sections.title: Behavioral and STAR Stories
sections.intro: These stories are drafts built from your resume (October 2026). Rewrite them in your own words so they sound natural out loud. For each story, know the Situation, Task, Action, and Result, plus one number you can quote.

cards.q: Tell Me About Yourself
cards.a:
Word-for-word script (about 60 seconds):

Hi, I'm Armaan. I'm a mechanical engineering senior at UCLA, and I graduate in June 2027.

Right now I'm the suspension and steering lead for Bruin Baja SAE. I lead a team of thirteen engineers, and I'm responsible for the entire system, front and rear: the geometry, the load cases, the analysis, building everything in-house, and testing it, all on a ten-thousand-dollar budget.

A big part of my job is making sure our design decisions come from real data. For example, we ran a roll-gradient test to set our camber gain target, and we drop-tested the car with an accelerometer so we're sizing parts against loads we actually measured, instead of numbers passed down from older teams. I also wrote SolidWorks macros that sweep the suspension through its full travel and steering range, so we catch interferences on the screen instead of on the car.

This year, that's put us on track for a system about ten percent lighter, including a steering rack that's twenty-one percent lighter with more travel. And I presented our design in New York, where we placed fourteenth out of over a hundred teams.

Before I was lead, I was on the shop floor building A-arms and machining parts myself, and I've taken that same design-to-build approach into combat robotics and a mechanical engineering internship at a robotics startup.

So I'm looking for a role where I can own hardware from the load case all the way through test, and that's exactly the kind of work your team does on [their product].

Short version (about 15 seconds)

I'm Armaan, a mechanical engineering senior at UCLA. I'm the suspension and steering lead for Bruin Baja SAE, where I lead thirteen engineers and own the system end to end: geometry, load cases, analysis, manufacturing, and testing. I'm looking for a role where I can take hardware from the load case all the way through test.

Swap the last line for the role

Structures: "So I'm looking for a structures role where I'm sizing parts against real load cases and proving them out with analysis and test."

Design: "So I'm looking for a design role where I own a subsystem from requirements all the way through build and validation."

Manufacturing: "So I'm looking for a role close to the build, where design decisions come from how the part actually gets made."

Delivery

  • Pause after each paragraph.
  • Every bold phrase is a hook they will ask about; know each one cold.
  • Fill in the company line before every interview.

cards.q: Baja SAE: Suspension Lead (M26)
cards.a:
• Situation: Lead of the suspension and steering subteam for the M26 vehicle, May 2026 to present.
  • Task: Deliver the full suspension and steering system (design, analysis, fabrication, validation) and integrate it with the other subsystems.
  • Action: Directing 13 project engineers, optimizing suspension geometry for mass and reliability, managing a $10,000 budget, working with FOX on shock procurement, and defending the design at formal technical reviews and competition design presentations.
  • Result: A system about 10% lighter and more reliable than its predecessor. Add competition results and test data once you have them.
  • Use for: leadership, managing people, budget and tradeoffs, communicating with other teams, defending a design decision.

cards.q: Baja SAE: Suspension Engineer (M25)
cards.a:
• Situation: Suspension team engineer, September 2025 to May 2026.
  • Action, fabrication: Built upper and lower A-arms using angle-grinder tube notching, DXF templates, and dedicated jigs. Machined tight-tolerance spacers and bushings on the manual mill and lathe.
  • Action, centerlock: Made a limit switch plate for the centerlock in Fusion CAM, holding critical bores to 0.001 to 0.002 in. Also designed a scaled centerlock hardware testbench so software and electrical could validate control logic and sensor behavior without the full vehicle. It used 3D-printed parts to keep cost down and a lead-screw-driven, axially adjustable limit switch mount so the controls team could tune trigger positions.
  • Action, failure response: Helped redesign an upper A-arm after a late-season critical failure, 3D printing test models to validate the new geometry.
  • Result: The testbench separated software development from the vehicle build schedule. Building it exposed alignment, backlash, and assembly issues that weren't visible in CAD.
  • Use for: failure (A-arm), tolerances (bores to 1 to 2 thou, testbench backlash), hands-on manufacturing, designing for a team's needs.
  • Fill in: what caused the A-arm failure, how you found the root cause, and what changed in the redesign. This is your best failure story, so know it cold.

cards.q: Advanced Spade Company Internship
cards.a:
• Situation: Mechanical engineering intern, May to September 2026.
  • Gimbal: Redesigned a pitch/roll camera gimbal for a sewer-inspection robot. Cut package volume 53% by re-tuning the gear ratio, supporting the roll shaft on ball bearings, and integrating a slip ring, with Teensy 4.1 control.
  • GNSS device: Led mechanical design across three phases of an in-house GNSS positioning device, from a retrofitted test fixture to a complete four-board production unit with a custom 2s2p battery pack.
  • Other: Redesigned the external battery charger enclosure, built a T-slot testbench mobility cart, and maintained a 12-printer automated print farm running 100+ hours a week.
  • Use for: real industry experience, packaging under tight constraints, ownership across a product's life, working with electronics.

subs.title: Combat Robotics: SKULL CRUSHER (Flagship, UCLA ASME)

cards.q: Combat Robotics: SKULL CRUSHER (Flagship, UCLA ASME)
cards.a:
• Situation: Weapon engineer on a 30 lb combat robot with a 12 lb weapon allocation.
  • Task: Maximize stored energy and survivability within the mass budget.
  • Action: Optimized weapon geometry for weight while meeting hit targets. Ran ANSYS FEA across revisions (bending, torsion, impact-type loading) to validate the spline hub. Critical regions were near the bore and attachment points, which drove fillet and thickness changes. Did topology studies on the side rails. Machined the hub spline, weapon shaft, motor shaft, and pulleys on manual and CNC mills and programmed the spline toolpaths in Fusion CAM. Designed for quick part swaps between fights.
  • Result: Placed 3rd of 12 teams.
  • Use for: FEA, design under a mass budget, dynamic and impact loads, design for maintenance.

cards.q: Combat Robotics: U.A.A.O.D.A.D. (UCLA Combat Robotics)
cards.a:
• Situation: Lead engineer on a 3 lb combat robot, designed and built in one week (May 2026).
  • Action: Parameterized the eggbeater weapon geometry and ran a weight-versus-energy sweep to size the disc within a 0.7 lb target while clearing a 300 J minimum. Machined the weapon and drivetrain on manual and CNC mills, then harnessed and soldered the full electrical system in a 12-hour push before competition.
  • Result: Finished and competed with the robot.
  • Use for: tight deadlines, fast iteration, prioritization, working outside mechanical.

subs.title: Crush Depth MATE ROV: FLOAT Lead

cards.q: Crush Depth MATE ROV: FLOAT Lead
cards.a:
• Situation: Lead mechanical engineer for an underwater vertical profiling float, leading a team of 4.
  • Task: Build a buoyancy engine and housing that cycles up and down repeatedly without leaking, using mostly 3D-printed parts.
  • Action: Iterated eight buoyancy and housing assemblies in SolidWorks. Dealt with 3D-print issues (layer adhesion, surface roughness, dimensional accuracy) using acetone vapor smoothing to improve finish and close micro-leak paths. Designed an O-ring interface at about 25% compression with heat-set threaded inserts and bolted clamping for even sealing pressure.
  • Result: Depth tested at 3.0 m for 150+ hours with zero leakage, a 90% improvement over previous years. Submitted to the 2025 MATE ROV Explorer Class Championship.
  • Use for: hard problem solved end to end, testing and validation, leading a small team.

If they ask about pressure loads: you validated by test rather than a full pressure model. The quick calc is hydrostatic pressure P = P_atm + ρgh. At 3 m that's ρgh ≈ 1000 × 9.81 × 3 ≈ 29 kPa (about 4.3 psi) above atmospheric. Use that ΔP to check housing wall stress and how much clamping force the seal needs.

cards.q: Common Behavioral Questions
cards.a:
Which story to reach for:

  • Describe a hard problem you solved end to end: FLOAT waterproofing, or the Advanced Spade gimbal redesign.
  • Tell me about a failure: Baja upper A-arm late-season failure and redesign.
  • Leadership: Baja Suspension Lead (13 engineers, $10,000 budget, design reviews).
  • Tight deadline: U.A.A.O.D.A.D. built in one week, 12-hour electrical push.
  • Tolerances causing a manufacturing problem: centerlock limit switch plate bores at 0.001 to 0.002 in, or testbench alignment and backlash.
  • Designing under constraints: SKULL CRUSHER 12 lb weapon budget, or the 53% smaller gimbal.
  • Disagreement with a teammate: not written yet. Pick a real Baja design disagreement and how it got resolved.
  • A design you would change: not written yet. A good option is something from M25 you changed on M26.

subs.title: What Are You Looking Forward to Learning?

cards.q: What Are You Looking Forward to Learning?
cards.a: I want to learn how the hands-on design and fabrication I've done in student projects and my internship scales up to flight-critical or production hardware. I've worked on parts that had to meet weight, strength, and packaging limits, and I want to see how those tradeoffs get made when the stakes and the system complexity are much higher. In particular: how large structures are analyzed and validated, how designs evolve through testing, how manufacturing shapes the final geometry, and how teams move fast without losing reliability.

cards.q: Questions to Ask the Interviewer
cards.a:
• What does success look like for a new engineer on this team in the first six months?
  • What are the biggest technical challenges the team is working on right now?
  • What kinds of parts or structures would I most likely own?
  • How closely do design engineers work with technicians on the floor?
  • What do you wish new hires already knew coming in?
  • What excites you most about the team's work right now?

sections.title: Resume Deep Dive
sections.intro: Questions a hiring engineer would ask after reading your resume and armaandhah.github.io, line by line. Answers use only what you've published. Have ready lists the numbers and details you need to know cold that aren't written down anywhere I can see. If you can't fill one in, that's the line to study before the interview. Rule of thumb: anything on the page is fair game, and every number invites "how did you get that?"

subs.title: Baja SAE Lead: Suspension Geometry and Steering

cards.q: Walk me through your M26 suspension design. What were the goals and how did you set them?
cards.a:
Every goal came back to two things: cut weight and raise reliability. M25 had three specific problems: interferences that only showed up on the built car (tie rod vs A-arm, tie rod vs rim, shock mount vs CV), steering effort that drivers complained about, and an A-arm that took three redesigns to hold up. So the M26 priorities were: validate geometry through travel before anything gets cut, lower steering effort and play, size parts against real loads instead of legacy ones, and get the subsystem about 10% lighter.

The design is still in progress, so I talk about it as targets and the analysis behind them, not test results yet.

Have ready

  • Front and rear architecture: double A-arm front? trailing arm with camber links rear? Say it in one sentence.
  • Wheelbase, track width, ride height, wheel travel (bump/droop), and tire size.
  • Your static camber, toe, caster (6.4°), kingpin inclination, and scrub radius.
  • What the 10% is measured against (M25 subsystem mass?) and the actual masses.

Where they'll push next

  • Why that architecture and not the alternative?
  • What would you change if you had another month?
  • What's the biggest risk left in the design?

cards.q: You wrote a VBA macro to sweep the geometry. How does it work, and why not just use Lotus or Optimum Kinematics?
cards.a:
I modeled the suspension in SolidWorks and wrote VBA macros that step the shock and rack through their travel. At each step the model rebuilds and the macro records camber gain, bump steer, turn angle, Ackermann percentage, turn radius, and clearances. That gave the team a validated way to catch interferences on screen instead of on the car, which no previous UCLA Baja team had.

The reason for doing it in SolidWorks rather than a kinematics package: our interference problems were with real 3D parts (tie rod vs rim, shock mount vs CV), and a hardpoint-only kinematics tool doesn't see part bodies. SolidWorks has the actual geometry, and the team already lives in it.

Have ready

  • How the macro drives travel: changing a driving dimension, a mate, or the Equations Manager? How many steps per sweep?
  • How it checks clearance: interference detection, or measuring minimum distance between bodies?
  • How you validated the macro itself (hand check of one position, compare against the M25 car, or against a kinematics tool)?
  • How long a full sweep takes to run.

Where they'll push next

  • How do you know the macro's numbers are right?
  • What's the resolution of your sweep, and could you miss an interference between steps?
  • What did it catch that you'd have missed otherwise?

cards.q: Define bump steer, camber gain, and Ackermann. What values did you aim for and why?
cards.a:
Bump steer is toe change as the wheel moves up and down. You want it near zero so the car doesn't steer itself over bumps, which matters a lot on Baja terrain. It's set mostly by where the tie rod's inner and outer points sit relative to the A-arms: if the tie rod isn't on the right line, it traces a different arc and pulls the wheel.

Camber gain is how camber changes with travel. Some negative camber gain in bump keeps the outside tire flatter in roll. On a Baja car with long travel it's a compromise, because large camber change also scrubs the tire over rough ground.

Ackermann is how much more the inside wheel steers than the outside in a turn, so both wheels roll around the same center without scrubbing. 100% means true Ackermann geometry; less is partial Ackermann.

Have ready

  • Your target and achieved bump steer (deg or in of toe per inch of travel).
  • Camber gain numbers in bump and droop.
  • Your Ackermann percentage and why you chose it.

Where they'll push next

  • How do you fix bump steer?
  • Why not 100% Ackermann?
  • How does camber gain interact with roll center height?

cards.q: Your goal was an 8 ft turn radius with no tire slip, which needed 37° of inside steer. How did you get 37°?
cards.a:
For a no-slip turn, both front wheels have to point at the same turn center on the rear axle line. With wheelbase L, front track t, and turn radius R measured to the vehicle centerline at the rear axle, tan(δ_inside) = L / (R − t/2) and tan(δ_outside) = L / (R + t/2). Running the numbers for an 8 ft turn radius with our wheelbase gave about 37° on the inside wheel, with the outside wheel smaller per Ackermann.

Pushing to 37° also pushed the worst-case turn angle with clearance to 43° at full bump, which is exactly where interferences show up, so I built a macro that checked every clearance through both steer and travel and iterated the geometry until it passed.

Have ready

  • Your wheelbase, front track, and exactly how you defined the 8 ft radius (to the outside wheel? the vehicle center?). Interviewers will check your 37° on the spot.
  • Outside wheel angle at full lock.
  • Where the 43° worst case comes from (steer plus bump-induced toe change?).

Where they'll push next

  • Is 'no tire slip' realistic? Tires always run some slip angle under lateral load. (Honest answer: it's the kinematic target at low speed.)
  • What limits the max steer angle: CV joint angle, tie rod-to-rim clearance, or the rack?

cards.q: Why did lowering caster to 6.4° reduce steering effort? What did you give up?
cards.a:
Caster tilts the steering axis back. That creates mechanical trail: the tire contact patch sits behind where the steering axis hits the ground, so the tire's side force has a lever arm that resists steering and pulls the wheel back to center. Less caster means less trail, so less effort and less kickback.

The tradeoff: less self-centering and straight-line stability, and less beneficial camber gain when you steer (caster makes the outside wheel gain negative camber in a turn). Kingpin inclination and scrub radius also feed into steering effort, so caster wasn't the only lever.

Have ready

  • M25's caster for comparison, and how much effort dropped (measured or calculated?).
  • Your kingpin inclination and scrub radius.
  • Whether drivers have felt the change yet, or if it's still on paper.

Where they'll push next

  • What's mechanical trail vs pneumatic trail?
  • Why not go to zero caster?

cards.q: Walk me through the M26 steering rack. How did you get more travel in a shorter package and cut 21% of the mass?
cards.a:
M25's steering had play, and its rack could rotate inside the housing, wearing the teeth unevenly. M26 locks rack alignment with a key, a pin, and a set screw adjustable from outside the housing, and a flat on the housing plus its mounting tabs stops the housing from rotating. That flat also let us remove a weight-adding step in the housing.

Rack travel goes from 2.48 to 3.37 in, in a package 0.6 in shorter. Lock to lock is 193°, under the 200° target. The assembly drops from 3.27 to 2.58 lb, about 21% lighter. I reviewed the FEA and hand calcs behind the new rack diameter and housing before committing to it.

Have ready

  • Rack ratio (c-factor): 3.37 in over 193° is about 6.3 in of travel per pinion revolution, so a pinion pitch diameter near 2 in. Know your actual pinion: teeth, module/diametral pitch, pitch diameter.
  • How you got more travel in a shorter housing (shorter non-toothed sections? different end stops?).
  • The rack load case: the tie rod force from your shear pin test, resolved into the rack-perpendicular bending load.
  • Rack and housing materials, and what the FEA showed (peak stress, margin).

Where they'll push next

  • Why does a rack rotating in its housing wear teeth unevenly?
  • Where is backlash coming from, and how does a key fix it?
  • What sets the 200° lock-to-lock target?

cards.q: You removed M25's tie rod extender. How did geometry let you do that, and why does it matter?
cards.a:
Optimizing the steering geometry put the tie rod points where they needed to be without an extra part, so the extender went away. That's one less part to carry and one less joint that can loosen or fail, which hits both of our goals, weight and reliability, at once.

Have ready

  • What the extender was compensating for on M25 (bump steer? clearance?).
  • Mass saved.

Where they'll push next

  • Any downside to the new tie rod location?

subs.title: Baja SAE Lead: Loads, Sizing, and Validation

cards.q: How do you know what loads to design the suspension for?
cards.a:
That's exactly the gap we're closing. A load case calculator is being built to solve component loads across bump, cornering, braking, acceleration, and impact directly from the SolidWorks geometry, so every part is designed against real numbers instead of legacy ones. Over-built parts carry mass for nothing; under-built ones fail.

The plan is to get real data: accelerometers and IMUs on the car, plus strain gauge impact testing on M25, and feed that back into M26.

Have ready

  • The g-levels you use for each case (e.g. bump, cornering, braking) and where they come from.
  • How the calculator turns a tire load into member forces (static equilibrium at the upright with the A-arm/link geometry? a free-body per corner?).
  • Bugs you found auditing the old load case sheet (you found lateral load transfer errors and a degrees-to-radians error in a bolt tear-out calc). This is a great story: it shows you check other people's numbers.

Where they'll push next

  • How would you validate the calculator?
  • Where would you put strain gauges on a control arm, and why?
  • How do you handle a dynamic impact load in a static calc? (dynamic factor, or energy method)

cards.q: Tell me about the lug calculator. What is the Air Force lug method?
cards.a:
Lugs sized without known loads get oversized. I used the Air Force lug method (from the published literature) to build a spreadsheet that sizes the steering clevis lugs to their real loads. The method checks the lug in axial loading (net-section tension and shear-bearing/tear-out), in transverse loading, and then combines them for an oblique load with an interaction equation.

Against the 680 lb measured in M25 testing with a 1.5 factor of safety, the lugs show a 1.23 margin, which leaves room to shrink the clevis further, and it's already about 35% lighter than M25's. I set it up as a copy-and-use template so anyone on the team can run lug checks the same way.

Have ready

  • Be precise about '1.23 margin': is it allowable/required = 1.23 (so margin of safety MS = 0.23), or MS = 1.23? Interviewers will ask, and the two mean very different things.
  • The interaction equation you used (the standard one is R_axial^1.6 + R_transverse^1.6 ≤ 1).
  • Lug material, thickness, hole and edge distance (e/D), and whether you checked pin bending and bushing bearing too.
  • How the 680 lb was measured on M25.

Where they'll push next

  • Why a 1.5 factor of safety and not 2?
  • What failure mode governed?
  • Why does the method treat axial and transverse loads separately?

cards.q: You moved the rear camber links from welded 4130 tube to 7075 billet. Defend that.
cards.a:
It cut about 20% of the link weight, removed weld heat-affected zones, and roughly tripled bending yield. Welds in 4130 tube are a known weak spot: the HAZ loses strength and is where fatigue cracks start, so a one-piece billet part takes that risk out.

Have ready

  • How 'tripled bending yield' was calculated (section modulus × yield, for which cross-sections?).
  • Axial and buckling stiffness: aluminum's E is about 1/3 of steel's. A link 20% lighter in a material 1/3 as dense has roughly 2.2× the area, so about 75–80% of the axial stiffness (if it were a solid-for-tube swap; check your real sections). Know whether you checked stiffness and compression buckling.
  • How the link attaches to steel rod ends (galvanic corrosion, thread engagement in aluminum, inserts?).
  • That you plan to buy 7075 rod and test it on the M25 car first.

Where they'll push next

  • 7075 has no endurance limit and is notch-sensitive. How do you handle fatigue?
  • Stress corrosion cracking in 7075-T6?
  • Why not 6061, or keep steel and fix the weld?
  • Does lower stiffness change the suspension compliance/handling?

cards.q: You moved the rear trailing arm from a CNC'd shock pocket to bolt-on brackets. What was the tradeoff?
cards.a:
Hitting the weight target meant the trailing arm couldn't keep its CNC'd shock pocket. Moving to bolt-on shock brackets let most of the part run on the waterjet with two mirrored CNC setups instead of one complex one. Simpler manufacturing and less mass, at the cost of adding a bolted joint.

Have ready

  • Mass saved on the trailing arm.
  • How the bolted bracket joint is sized (bolt shear and bearing, preload, double shear?) and how you'll keep it from loosening.

Where they'll push next

  • Isn't a bolted joint less reliable than a machined pocket?
  • How do you locate the bracket accurately?

cards.q: How did you pick spring rates? What's motion ratio, and how does your dual-rate setup work?
cards.a:
A spring rate picked by feel risks a car that bottoms out and breaks parts, or one so stiff it needs heavier hardware. I built a dual-rate spring calculator around the FOX dual-rate shock, working from motion ratio (shock travel over wheel travel) to the spring rates the car actually needs. It lives in a Google Sheet with a step-by-step guide so future leads pick springs from math.

Wheel rate = spring rate × MR² (times cos² of the shock's installation angle if MR is just the lever ratio). It's squared because the lever changes both the force and the displacement. A dual-rate shock stacks two springs in series: both compress at first, giving a softer combined rate k₁k₂/(k₁ + k₂), then a crossover stop locks out the softer spring and the rate jumps to the stiffer one. Soft for small bumps, firm before bottoming.

Have ready

  • Your motion ratio front and rear, the spring rates you landed on, and the crossover point.
  • Ride frequency target (wheel rate and corner sprung mass give f = (1/2π)√(k/m)).
  • The FOX shock model (885-06-161 dual rate) and what data you asked FOX for (CAD, weight, damping).

Where they'll push next

  • Why is motion ratio squared?
  • How do you choose damping?
  • What's a typical ride frequency for an off-road car vs a road car?

cards.q: Your resume says 'significantly more reliable than its predecessor.' The car isn't built. How can you claim that?
cards.a:
Fair challenge. Honestly, it's a design claim backed by analysis, not test data yet. What supports it: the parts that failed or wore on M25 have been addressed directly (the rack can no longer rotate and wear its teeth unevenly, the tie rod extender joint is gone, welded camber links are now one-piece billet), interferences are checked through full travel and steer in CAD before manufacturing, and parts are being sized against measured loads (like the 680 lb steering load) instead of guesses. The real proof will be testing, which is why we're instrumenting M25 now.

Have ready

  • One concrete M25 failure and exactly what in M26 prevents it.

Where they'll push next

  • What test will prove it?
  • What's your definition of reliability: no failures across an endurance race? Mean distance between failures?

subs.title: Baja SAE: Leadership, Budget, and Fabrication

cards.q: How do you manage 13 engineers? Give me a specific example of a conflict or a missed deadline.
cards.a:
Speak to how you split the work (by component? by phase?), how you track it, and how you review designs before they get cut. Then one specific story: a disagreement over a design, someone who fell behind, or a part that came back wrong, and what you did.

Have ready

  • Your structure: who owns what, how often you meet, how you track tasks.
  • One real conflict story with a clear outcome.
  • How you develop newer members (the documentation templates and copy-and-use calculators are a good answer).

Where they'll push next

  • How do you handle someone who isn't pulling their weight?
  • Have you ever had to overrule someone? Were you right?

cards.q: How do you manage a $10,000 budget? Where did M25 go over?
cards.a:
Know the split by category, how purchases get approved, and what you learned from M25's actuals. M25 spent about $10K with notable overruns in bearings and rod ends; M26's target is around $10.3K.

Have ready

  • Biggest line items (shocks, rod ends, bearings, stock material).
  • What you cut or deferred to stay on budget.
  • How sponsorships or donated material factor in.

Where they'll push next

  • If you had $2,000 more, where would it go?
  • How do you weigh cost against weight savings?

cards.q: You presented at competition design and placed 14th of 100+. What did the judges ask, and what would you change?
cards.a:
By the second competition I'd been named M26 lead, so I gave the design presentation in New York, where we placed 14th in design out of over 100 teams.

Have ready

  • Two or three questions judges actually asked and how you answered.
  • The weakest part of your presentation in hindsight.

Where they'll push next

  • What do design judges care about most: the numbers, or the process behind them?

cards.q: How do you hold tolerance when notching and welding A-arm tube? How does weld distortion affect geometry?
cards.a:
I notched tube stock with an angle grinder, laying out simpler notches with a protractor and pulling complex ones off DXF templates, then built dedicated jigs to hold each part, because suspension geometry is very sensitive to misalignment. The jig fixes the critical points (ball joint and pivot locations) so the part can't move while it's tacked and welded.

Have ready

  • What tolerance you held on the hardpoints and how you measured it.
  • Whether you did the welding (TIG is on your resume) and how you managed distortion: tack sequence, alternating sides, letting it cool in the jig.
  • Tube material, OD, and wall.

Where they'll push next

  • Why does weld distortion happen?
  • What's the effect of a pivot being 1/16 in off?
  • Why angle grinder over a tube notcher?

cards.q: You held the centerlock limit switch bores to 1–2 thou. How, and how did you measure it?
cards.a:
I programmed the toolpaths in Fusion CAM and held the limit switch bores to 1–2 thou for a near-perfect fit, since a sloppy fit there is the kind of reliability problem that shows up at the worst time.

Have ready

  • How you cut the bores (helical interpolation? bore then finishing pass? reamer?).
  • How you measured them (pin gauges, bore gauge, calipers aren't good enough for 0.001).
  • Material, tool, and feeds/speeds.
  • Whether 1–2 thou means ±0.001–0.002 or total, and on what nominal.

Where they'll push next

  • What's the difference between accuracy and repeatability on a mill?
  • Why might a bore come out undersized on a CNC?

cards.q: A late-season A-arm failed. What was the root cause, and how do you know the redesign fixed it?
cards.a:
Late in the season an A-arm failed, so I helped redesign it from the ground up. Before committing to the new geometry I 3D-printed test models to check clearances and fit against the rest of the suspension without waiting on another metal build.

Have ready

  • The actual failure: where it broke, the failure mode (fatigue crack at a weld? overload? buckling?) and the root cause. This is the first thing they'll ask.
  • What changed in the redesign to address that cause specifically.
  • How it held up afterward.

Where they'll push next

  • How can a plastic print validate 'vehicle dynamics'? (Be careful: it validates geometry and clearance, not strength or dynamics.)
  • What would you do differently to catch this earlier?

cards.q: Walk me through the gimbal redesign. How did you cut package volume 53%?
cards.a:
I picked up an unfinished pitch/roll prototype for the CRABCAKE sewer-inspection robot and carried it to a working redesign. The roll shaft runs in a mounted ball bearing sized for a 5/8 in shaft, then steps down to 9.5 mm at the driven gear. I used the motor already on hand with a 1:3 ratio (20 teeth driving 60), which kept the camera moving fast while drawing about a watt. A 12-channel slip ring allows continuous 360° roll. Control runs on a Teensy 4.1 reading one joystick. Altogether the package shrank 53%.

Have ready

  • Before and after envelope dimensions, and which change saved the most volume.
  • Output speed and torque at the camera (motor speed ÷ 3; torque × 3 minus losses).
  • Why a slip ring instead of a cable wrap with limited rotation.

Where they'll push next

  • How did you measure 'about a watt'?
  • What's the camera's inertia and how fast does it need to move?
  • How would you seal this for a sewer environment?

cards.q: You bored a gear out on a drill press. How did you keep it concentric?
cards.a:
Metal gears for a 3 mm motor shaft only came in one bore size, so I bored the driven gear out to 9.5 mm myself on a drill press.

Have ready

  • How you located the gear on center (a fixture? a center drill first? a pilot hole and step drills?).
  • Runout you saw, and whether it mattered (gear noise, backlash variation, binding).
  • How the gear is fixed to the shaft (set screw? key? press fit?).

Where they'll push next

  • A drill press isn't a precision tool. What would you use with more time? (Lathe with a collet or 4-jaw, then ream.)
  • What happens to gear mesh if the bore is off-center?

cards.q: How do the pitch soft and hard limits work, and why set them inside the mechanical stops?
cards.a:
Pitch is mechanically limited to about 180° and capped in software using the pitch encoder's count: a soft limit and a tighter hard limit, both set inside the true mechanical stops. The axis can only ever be blocked from moving outward, never trapped against a stop, so the motor never stalls into a hard stop. A re-zero button lets the operator redefine center after manually returning the arm to true zero.

Have ready

  • Encoder type and resolution.
  • What happens on power-up: does it assume it's at zero?
  • What the difference between your soft and hard limit actually does.

Where they'll push next

  • What happens if the encoder slips or loses count?
  • Would you add a homing switch?

cards.q: Explain the GNSS device you worked on. What is RTK, and why did the IMU/antenna offsets matter?
cards.a:
The Positioning Cell Initiative was the company's own RTK GNSS device, and my job across three phases was to give firmware and electrical a mechanical platform to test against. Phase 1: a fast retrofit of an existing CRKT unit with a survey-pole adapter that raised the antenna for a cleaner fix, using a print-pause 5/8-11 coupling nut as the attachment point. Phase 2: a four-piece modular test rig (the 'sceptre') holding IMUs, breakouts, and a dev kit. Phase 3: the first complete four-board unit (positioning, main, interface, BMS), shaped around the company logo's triangular form.

RTK GNSS gets centimeter-level position by using corrections from a fixed base station. The position you care about is the pole tip, not the antenna, so every offset between antenna, IMU, and tip has to be known. The Phase 2 frame held zero offset in every direction except vertical, which kept the RTK math simple and cut firmware setup time.

Have ready

  • What the device was for (surveying? robot localization?).
  • Why a tilted pole needs the IMU (tilt compensation of the lever arm).

Where they'll push next

  • Why does the antenna height off the ground help the fix (multipath, sky view)?
  • How did you hold the alignment tolerances in a 3D-printed frame?

cards.q: What's a 'print-pause coupling nut' and why use it?
cards.a:
You pause the 3D print at the layer just above the nut pocket, drop a steel 5/8-11 coupling nut in, and resume. The printer encapsulates it, so you get a strong steel thread fully captured in plastic with no adhesive or heat-set insert. I used it for the survey-pole attachment and reused it through all three phases.

Where they'll push next

  • How strong is it vs a heat-set insert?
  • What goes wrong with print-pause (layer adhesion over the nut, nut not seated flat)?

cards.q: You designed a 2s2p battery pack. What does 2s2p mean, and what did you have to think about?
cards.a:
2s2p is two series groups of two parallel cells (or equivalently two series strings tied in parallel): double the cell voltage and double the cell capacity. I drafted the schematic, built the first pack using the same cells as the CRKT packs, and helped bring up the BMS board, hand-soldering surface-mount parts on it.

Have ready

  • Cell chemistry and form factor, nominal pack voltage (about 7.2–7.4 V for Li-ion) and capacity.
  • How you joined cells (spot welding nickel strip is on your resume) and why you don't solder directly to cells.
  • What the BMS does: over/under-voltage, over-current, balancing the two series groups, temperature.
  • Fusing and how you insulated and retained the pack mechanically.

Where they'll push next

  • Why must parallel cells be at the same voltage before connecting?
  • What happens if one series group drifts?
  • How do you keep a pack from shorting if the device is dropped?

cards.q: How did you design for assembly on the tapered four-board unit?
cards.a:
The triangular, tapered form made assembly order sensitive, so I wrote out a specific upside-down, bottom-up build sequence so the boards, ribbon cables, and battery pack went in correctly every time. I worked board-level layout with our PCB designer in Altium Co-Designer, moving models back and forth with SolidWorks.

Have ready

  • One example of a mechanical constraint you pushed back to the electrical side (connector location, board outline, keep-out).
  • What Altium Co-Designer actually does in the workflow (ECAD-MCAD collaboration: sharing the board outline, component heights, mounting holes).

Where they'll push next

  • What would you change to make it easier to assemble?
  • How do you handle tolerance between a PCB and a printed enclosure?

cards.q: Tell me about the battery charger enclosure and the testbench cart.
cards.a:
Charger: built around a new single-slot charger board, with a commercial light pipe for the status LED, a solid-infill upper section to weight the base, and corner-bolted rubber feet that clamp the base plate and battery retention together in one fastening step. I tuned battery retention with an Excel-driven design table in SolidWorks, sweeping the pocket offset until it converged on a reliable slip fit.

Cart: a lab testbench was fully stationary, so I designed a caster cart that matches its height with custom-cut T-slot extrusion and reuses its rail profile and spacing so a heavy baseplate rolls straight across. The cart's T-slot geometry tracks into the bench's open slots as it rolls up, so alignment is self-guiding, and four total-lock casters lock rotation and swivel once it's seated, for a stable single-operator transfer.

Have ready

  • What slip-fit clearance you landed on for the battery (and why printed parts need a different clearance than nominal).
  • Baseplate weight and the cart's tipping check.

Where they'll push next

  • Why do total-lock casters matter vs normal brakes?
  • How did you check the cart wouldn't tip during transfer?

cards.q: You maintained a 12-printer farm running 100+ hours a week. What does 'maintained' mean in practice?
cards.a:
Know what you actually did: queueing and slicing jobs, calibration, nozzle and bed maintenance, material management, troubleshooting failures, and keeping the farm fed for the whole product line.

Have ready

  • Printer models and software (OctoPrint? a farm manager?).
  • The most common failure and how you fixed it.
  • Materials you ran and why (PLA, PETG, ABS, TPU).

Where they'll push next

  • How do you design a part to print well (overhangs, orientation, tolerances, layer direction vs load)?

cards.q: How did you optimize the weapon geometry within the 12 lb allocation?
cards.a:
I worked in a four-person subteam and took the initial weapon design through iteration: adapting it for clearances and trimming weight out of the disk and hub so the assembly hit its speed target without breaking the 12 lb weapon allocation, while keeping the original performance goals. Stored energy is ½Iω², so mass far from the axis is what stores energy. You trim mass near the hub, where it adds weight but little inertia, and keep it at the rim and the teeth.

Have ready

  • The weapon's moment of inertia and stored energy at 10,000 rpm (E = ½Iω²).
  • Disk material and how many blades/teeth.
  • What 'hit targets' meant in numbers.

Where they'll push next

  • Why is energy ∝ ω² important when choosing speed vs mass?
  • What's bite and why does it matter?
  • How do you balance a spinning weapon?

cards.q: You ran ANSYS FEA on the spline hub. What were the loads and boundary conditions, and how did you validate the results?
cards.a:
The hub had to survive direct hits from an opposing 30 lb robot. I ran ANSYS FEA across design revisions to check spline hub survivability.

Have ready

  • How you turned a hit into a load: an impact energy and stopping distance? a torque from the weapon decelerating? an assumed g-load?
  • Boundary conditions: what you fixed and where (shaft? bearings?), and why.
  • Mesh refinement at the spline roots, what the peak stress was vs yield, and how you treated singularities at sharp corners.
  • A hand calc you used to sanity-check it (shear stress on spline teeth: τ = 2T / (d·A_shear), or torsion Tc/J).

Where they'll push next

  • Static FEA for an impact load: is that valid?
  • How would you check the result is right?
  • Where did it want to fail, and what did you change?

cards.q: How did you machine the spline hub? What did you learn in Fusion CAM?
cards.a:
I learned Fusion CAM to program the spline hub on the CNC mill, and machined the weapon shaft, motor shaft, and pulleys.

Have ready

  • Internal or external spline, tooth count, and how you cut it on a mill (internal corners need an end mill radius, so the spline profile has to allow it).
  • Material, tools, and the toolpath strategy (adaptive clearing, contour finishing).
  • Fit between hub and shaft and how you checked it.

Where they'll push next

  • Why a spline instead of a key or set screw?
  • What's the fillet at the root of a milled internal spline, and how does it affect stress?

cards.q: How did you design for swapping parts between fights?
cards.a:
Every part of the weapon, hub to shaft, was designed to come apart quickly, so a damaged part could be pulled and replaced with a spare between rounds. The weapon spun to 10,000 rpm and held up through our fights with minimal weapon-side maintenance, mostly fresh blades between rounds. We placed 3rd of 12.

Have ready

  • The swap time between rounds and what fasteners you used.
  • How you kept bolts from backing out under impact (threadlocker, preload, safety wire).

cards.q: Explain your weight-vs-energy sweep. Why was the relationship linear?
cards.a:
One goal was at least 300 J of stored energy. We swept a parameterized eggbeater profile over length and width, logging moment of inertia and rotational energy (½Iω² at our set battery voltage and motor speed) for each combination. Plotted against weapon weight, energy came out roughly linear in mass, which let us pick a geometry that cleared 300 J with room to spare while keeping the disc under 0.7 lb.

Why linear: I ≈ m·k², where k is the radius of gyration. If most of the sweep changes width or thickness at a similar length, k barely changes, so I, and therefore energy at a fixed speed, scales with mass. Changing length would not be linear: a longer bar adds mass in proportion to length but inertia roughly with length cubed.

Have ready

  • The final disc dimensions, mass, I, and energy.
  • The speed you computed energy at (your calculated max is about 19,600 rpm).

Where they'll push next

  • If you had sized for energy per unit mass, which parameter would you change?
  • Was 300 J at full speed, or at the speed reached after spin-up?

cards.q: Walk me through the 1.429:1 pulley ratio and the 1.7 s spin-up. What's the tradeoff?
cards.a:
A 14-tooth pulley on the motor's 1/8 in shaft drives a 20-tooth pulley on the 1/4 in weapon shaft: a 1.429:1 reduction, set largely by which shaft and pulley sizes we could get within a week. That gave a calculated spin-up of about 1.7 s to a max of about 19,600 rpm.

The tradeoff: more reduction gives more torque at the weapon, so it reaches its own top speed faster, but that top speed is lower, and energy goes with speed squared. Less reduction gives a higher top speed and more energy at the hit, but slower spin-up. For reaching a fixed target speed there's a sweet spot in between, and too much reduction can't reach the target at all. Every time we pushed one, we lost the other.

Have ready

  • Motor KV and battery voltage (19,600 rpm × 1.429 ≈ 28,000 rpm at the motor).
  • How you calculated spin-up time: motor torque curve against weapon inertia reflected through the ratio.
  • Belt type (GT2/HTD?) and how you tensioned it.

Where they'll push next

  • Why did the shaft size limit the pulley choice?
  • Does the weapon actually reach no-load speed? (No: losses and battery sag.)

cards.q: Why hardened 4140 for the disc, TPU 98A for the chassis, and UHMW for the uprights?
cards.a:
Disc: hardened 4140 over annealed or aluminum for wear resistance and toughness, so the edge doesn't deform or crack after repeated full-speed hits. We took on machining hardened stock on a CNC mill with limited tooling. Chassis: a single-piece TPU 98A print, one of the more rigid TPUs, for impact toughness without multi-part assembly time. Uprights and top plate: UHMW for impact resistance and low weight, since they mainly locate the weapon shaft and keep things square. The waterjet was down, so we cut them from printed DXF templates on a bandsaw and finished the bores on the CNC.

Have ready

  • Hardness of the 4140 and what tooling you used.
  • Why not tool steel like S7 (common in combat robotics for its toughness)?

Where they'll push next

  • Hardened steel is harder but more brittle. How did you trade hardness against toughness?
  • How does UHMW hold a bearing bore over time (creep)?

cards.q: You competed with it. How did it do?
cards.a:
Be straight about it. We built a fully working 3 lb robot from scratch in one week, but the ESCs never got fully programmed in time. We got a successful weapon spin-up but had no meaningful control over it once it was running. What I'd fix first: the housing came out bulkier than needed and wasn't designed for assembly, and the electronics needed to arrive and be tested days earlier, not 12 hours before. That's why I now plan electrical integration and firmware time in from the start.

Where they'll push next

  • What would you do differently in the planning?
  • How do you decide when to cut scope under a deadline?

cards.q: How did you size the O-ring gland? Walk me through the numbers.
cards.a:
Seals had failed here in past years, so I ran the numbers myself. Using the standard compression formula, I sized the gland depth for 25% compression of the ring's cross-section, with groove width at 1.5× the cross-section so the compressed ring could spread instead of extruding out the sides, and fillets in every corner to protect the ring. I validated it with a test puck matching the housing diameter: a slow one-minute depth test and a fast, choppy depth-change test, zero leakage on both interfaces.

Have ready

  • The O-ring size, cross-section, and material/durometer (Buna-N 70A is typical).
  • Gland fill: with those proportions the ring fills about 70% of the groove, under the ~85–90% limit, so it has room for swell and thermal growth.
  • Face seal or radial (piston/bore) seal for each interface.
  • Surface finish on a 3D-printed sealing surface, and how you handled it.

Where they'll push next

  • Why 25% and not 40%?
  • What causes O-ring extrusion, and when do you need a backup ring?
  • Why does a gland need room to fill?

cards.q: 'Depth-tested to 3.0 m with zero leakage over 150+ hours, a 90% improvement over previous years.' 90% of what?
cards.a:
Know exactly what the 90% compares. Is it 90% fewer leaks? 90% longer time without a leak? 90% less water intrusion? An interviewer will ask, and a vague answer undercuts a strong project.

Also: 3 m of fresh water is only about 30 kPa (4.3 psi) of gauge pressure. Your hoop stress check at a simulated 20 m (about 0.2 MPa) gave a factor of safety around 12. Be ready to say the low pressure is why a printed housing can work at all, and what would change at 100 m.

Have ready

  • The baseline from previous years and how you measured it.
  • Whether 150+ hours was continuous or cumulative across tests.

Where they'll push next

  • At what depth would your design stop working, and what fails first?
  • Why did FDM housings leak, and why did vapor smoothing fix it?

cards.q: How did you make 3D-printed ABS housings waterproof?
cards.a:
FDM parts leak at the layer lines under pressure. Hand-brushing acetone blended the layers but was slow and inconsistent; a small vapor chamber worked on small parts but smoothed big housings unevenly. What worked was a flash vapor chamber sized for the housing itself: it smoothed a part in minutes with consistent results, so we could reprint, smooth, and pressure-test a new revision in a single day. The housing went through several iterations before it sealed reliably every time.

Have ready

  • Iteration count: your resume says eight assemblies, the portfolio says nine housing iterations. Pick the correct number and say it the same way everywhere.
  • Print settings that helped (wall count, infill, layer height, orientation).
  • Effect of vapor smoothing on dimensions (it rounds edges and can shift the O-ring groove).

Where they'll push next

  • Why not machine the housing or buy a commercial enclosure? (No machine shop in the program.)
  • Acetone vapor safety?

cards.q: How did you check that a scavenged stepper could drive the buoyancy engine?
cards.a:
We chose one large syringe with the lead screw inside it over a bank of smaller syringes: fewer seals, less friction, smaller package. With almost no budget, the motor was a stepper from an old 3D printer, so I checked it could do the job. I measured plunger friction with a force gauge, separating static breakaway from the steady kinetic force, added the water-pressure load at depth, applied a factor of safety of 2, then converted to torque through the lead screw's lead and an assumed efficiency: T = F·l / (2π·η). It came out close enough to the motor's rated holding torque to know it would work.

Have ready

  • The actual numbers: friction force, pressure load (p × plunger area), lead, assumed efficiency, required torque vs motor rating.
  • Holding torque vs running torque: a stepper's torque drops with speed, so holding torque is optimistic for a moving screw.

Where they'll push next

  • Why measure static and kinetic friction separately?
  • Is the lead screw back-drivable? Does that matter when the motor is unpowered at depth?

cards.q: How did you size the TPU feet? And the bolt pattern?
cards.a:
Feet: I worked backward from an impact-energy budget: estimated drop velocity from a drag balance, turned that into kinetic energy at impact, and compared the stopping force over a compliant foot's ~10 mm of give against a rigid ~1 mm contact, about a 10× lower impact force. Bolts: I checked the 10-bolt M4 pattern against the required clamping force for about a factor of safety of 3.

Have ready

  • The clamping force you needed and where it came from (O-ring compression force plus pressure on the lid).
  • Bolt preload assumption and torque.

Where they'll push next

  • Why does stopping distance matter so much? (F ≈ KE / d.)
  • Why not just make the housing stronger?

cards.q: How did you lead a team of four on this, with competition deadlines?
cards.a:
I supervised a team of four in CAD, fabrication, and mechanical testing to hit milestones, wrote the technical documentation of all design parameters, presented at the design presentation, and submitted the system to the 2025 MATE ROV Explorer Class Championship.

Have ready

  • One story about a missed milestone or a disagreement on the float team.
  • How you split the work between the four.

cards.q: You list TIG welding, spot welding, lathe, mill, and CNC. Rate yourself honestly on each.
cards.a:
Interviewers test the skills list by picking one and asking you to describe a real job on it. Rate yourself honestly (built a few parts vs could do it unsupervised), and have one specific part for each tool.

Have ready

  • A specific part for each: TIG (what joint, what material?), spot welding (the battery pack nickel strip?), lathe (spacers and bushings), manual mill, CNC (spline hub, limit switch plate, 4140 disc).
  • Speeds and feeds basics: why carbide vs HSS, what chatter is and how to fix it, climb vs conventional milling.

Where they'll push next

  • What's the difference between TIG, MIG, and stick?
  • How would you set up a part to face both sides parallel?

cards.q: You list FEA in ANSYS and SolidWorks. What's your process for setting up an analysis?
cards.a:
Geometry cleanup, material, loads and boundary conditions that match the real constraints, a mesh refined where stress concentrates, a convergence check, then compare to a hand calc before trusting it. Point to real uses: the Skull Crusher spline hub in ANSYS, reviewing the rack and housing FEA for M26, and multi-load-case setups in Ansys Mechanical.

Have ready

  • One analysis you can describe end to end with numbers.
  • A time FEA was wrong at first and how you caught it.

Where they'll push next

  • Force vs displacement boundary conditions: when do you use each?
  • What's a stress singularity?
  • Linear vs nonlinear analysis: when do you need nonlinear?

cards.q: What have you done in MATLAB, AutoCAD, and VBA?
cards.a:
VBA is easy: SolidWorks macros for the geometry sweep and hardpoint visualization, plus Excel design tables. Have a real example ready for MATLAB and AutoCAD, or be honest that they're coursework-level.

Have ready

  • A MATLAB script or analysis you wrote.
  • Where you used AutoCAD (DXF templates for notching and bandsaw cutting count).

cards.q: You transferred from community college. Why, and how was the jump to UCLA?
cards.a:
Short, positive story: what you did at Clovis (4.0, tutorial center team lead, MATE ROV), why you transferred, and how you got involved at UCLA fast (Baja member in Sept 2025, lead by May 2026).

Have ready

  • Why your GPA moved from 4.0 to 3.7 if they ask: say it plainly (harder upper-division load plus a heavy project schedule) without excuses.

Where they'll push next

  • What did tutoring teach you that helps you as an engineer?

cards.q: Your Baja lead role, internship, and a combat robot build all started in May 2026. How did you manage that?
cards.a:
Know your answer for the overlap: the internship was full-time May to September, the 3 lb robot was a one-week sprint in May, and the Baja lead role runs through the year. Explain how you prioritized and what you delegated.

Where they'll push next

  • How do you avoid spreading yourself too thin?
  • What did you drop when things collided?

cards.q: Of everything on your resume, what are you proudest of, and what would you do differently?
cards.a: Pick one project and own it end to end, with numbers. Then a real 'do differently' that shows learning, not a humble-brag. Good pairs: proudest of building a validation process (VBA sweep, lug calculator) the team never had; do differently: plan electrical integration earlier (U.A.A.O.D.A.D.) or catch the A-arm failure mode in analysis before it happened.

cards.q: Things on your resume a sharp interviewer will poke at
cards.a:
Fix these on the page or have a clean answer ready:

Have ready

  • "Ensure flawless vehicle integration": 'flawless' invites "so nothing ever interfered?" Consider 'reliable integration' or naming what you coordinate.
  • "Significantly more reliable" for M26, which isn't built yet. Have the analysis-based defense ready (see the reliability card above).
  • "90% improvement over previous years" on the FLOAT seal: define the metric, or reword it.
  • Iteration count: resume says eight buoyancy and housing assemblies; portfolio says nine housing iterations.
  • U.A.A.O.D.A.D. "competed with the finished robot": true, but the weapon couldn't be controlled. Lead with that yourself rather than having it found on your site.
  • Lug "1.23 margin": be precise whether that's a ratio or a margin of safety.
  • Gimbal bullet says 'ball-bearing-supported roll shaft': know the bearing part number and why that bearing.
  • Every number (53%, 10%, 21%, 35%, 20%, 680 lb, 300 J, 19,600 rpm, 10,000 rpm, 150+ hours, 12 printers): know how it was measured or calculated.

cards.q: How much of this did you do yourself vs your team?
cards.a:
Interviewers want to know your part. Use 'I' for what you did and 'we' for team work, and be specific. From your own site: on Skull Crusher you were one of four on the weapon subteam; on U.A.A.O.D.A.D. it was you and a teammate; on M26 you lead and review others' work (for example, you reviewed the rack FEA and hand calcs rather than running them yourself).

Have ready

  • For each bullet, one sentence on exactly what you did with your own hands or head.

sections.title: Mock Interview: Former Suspension Lead
sections.intro: From a full mock interview with a graduated Baja suspension lead who has interviewed at SpaceX and Tesla. It follows the real order: intro, resume deep dive, then technical problem sets that build one question at a time. Where your answer in the mock missed, the card gives the stronger answer.

cards.q: What did the mock interviewer say interviewers actually do?
cards.a:
They pick something on your resume, ask for a short summary, then start picking it apart, first a bullet point, then whatever you said in your answer. Every bullet and every design decision is fair game, including "why didn't you use this other design?" Know why you rejected the alternatives, not just what you chose.

Her advice

  • Project summaries: 2 to 3 minutes, hit the important parts, then let them ask follow-ups. Don't ramble for ten.
  • Technical questions build on each other. The first one is often genuinely simple. Don't second-guess it.
  • If they start asking leading follow-up questions, that's them steering you toward the answer. Stop defending your path, pause, and think about what they're hinting at.
  • If you don't know, work it out from fundamentals out loud. Interviewers like that more than a memorized answer.
  • Structures roles rarely ask fluids or thermal, but pressure vessels (hoop stress) are fair game, especially at SpaceX. For energy or space roles, know Bernoulli and heat transfer, especially radiation.
  • Know the core equations cold: σ = My/I, δ = PL³/3EI, σ_hoop = pr/t, σ_axial = pr/2t, T = KDP. Coefficients matter less than knowing how the variables scale.

cards.q: Do you have any questions for me?
cards.a:
Ask about what they're working on: the hardest technical problem on the team right now, or what they personally built recently. People like talking about their own work, it shows real interest, and it often fills the rest of the time. Prepare two or three in advance so you can actually listen to their answers instead of planning your next question.

Follow-ups

  • More options are on the Behavioral → Questions to Ask the Interviewer card.
  • Follow up on something they said earlier in the interview; it shows you were listening.

subs.title: Baja Deep Dive: Where It Got Hard

cards.q: How do you set your camber gain target?
cards.a:
Camber matters most for keeping the tire flat, and so grip, through cornering, when the body rolls. So we tied the target to how much the car actually rolls. We ran a roll-gradient test on a skid pad with an IMU to measure body roll versus lateral acceleration, and used that to set how much camber gain the geometry needs over the corresponding shock travel to keep the outside tire close to flat.

Then the geometry sweep (the VBA macro) checks camber gain and bump steer through full travel and steer against those targets.

Follow-ups

  • Know the roll gradient number (degrees of roll per g) and the resulting camber gain target.
  • Why not just maximize camber gain? On a Baja car with long travel, big camber change scrubs the tire over bumps and changes track width. It's a compromise.
  • How did you get lateral acceleration on the skid pad? (radius and lap time, or the IMU directly).

cards.q: How do you find your load cases? How do you know you're designing for the maximum load?
cards.a:
From testing plus competition experience. Former leads reported the worst drops at competition around 4 to 4.5 ft. We could test a 3.5 ft ledge on campus, so we mounted a phone IMU (the Phyphox app) to the chassis, measured the peak acceleration in g's, fed that into the load case calculator as a wheel acceleration, and applied a factor of safety of about 1.5 to cover the bigger drops.

Back it up with the math: impact speed is √(2gh), so 3.5 ft hits at about 15 ft/s and 4.5 ft at about 17 ft/s. That's 29% more energy, but for a roughly linear suspension the peak force only rises with speed, about 13%. A 1.5 factor covers that with margin, unless the suspension bottoms out, where the force spikes. That's the case to watch.

Follow-ups

  • "Is that your maximum or your 95th percentile?" Be honest: it's a measured case plus a factor, not a true maximum. The plan to instrument M25 (accelerometers, IMUs, strain gauges) is how you'd get the real distribution.
  • A phone IMU's sample rate and mounting can miss or smear a short impact peak. Mount it rigidly and know the sample rate.
  • Before this, loads were legacy values passed down for years. Saying you replaced them with measured data is a strong point.

cards.q: Your IMU was on the chassis. How do you know how much load goes through the unsprung suspension components?
cards.a:
This is the one that got me. Model a corner as a quarter car: the tire is a stiff spring, then the unsprung mass (wheel, upright, part of the links), then the shock (spring and damper), then the sprung mass (chassis). A chassis IMU measures the sprung mass, which the shock has already filtered. The unsprung mass moves at a much higher frequency (wheel hop, roughly 10 to 15 Hz versus 1 to 3 Hz for the body) and sees much higher accelerations.

What that means for loads: the force through the shock into the chassis is about m_sprung × a_chassis, which is what my calculator effectively used. But the tire contact force, and the loads on the upright, hub, and lower links, also include m_unsprung × a_wheel, plus any spike when the suspension bottoms. So the chassis-only method can underpredict the loads on unsprung parts.

Follow-ups

  • How I'd fix it: put an accelerometer on the upright too (unsprung), add shock potentiometers to get shock force directly from spring rate × travel plus damping × velocity, and put strain gauges on the links to measure the loads directly. That's exactly what the strain gauge plan is for.
  • The rear calculator treats the camber links and trailing arm as two-force members and solves statically. Say that out loud, and say what it ignores (link inertia, dynamic tire spring).
  • A Tesla interviewer asked the mock interviewer the same thing about shock pots: are you accounting for the different natural frequencies of the sprung and unsprung masses?

cards.q: Your FEA shows a very high stress in a tiny region. How do you know if it's real?
cards.a:
First, look at where it is. A single node at a sharp re-entrant corner, a point load, or a fixed constraint is usually a singularity. A real stress concentration covers a region with a smooth gradient around it. Then refine the mesh there: a real stress converges to a value, while a singularity keeps climbing every time you refine. Then check it with a hand calc (P/A, Mc/I, Kt × nominal) for the region around it. If that agrees, it's real; if the hand calc is way lower and the peak keeps growing with refinement, it's an artifact.

Follow-ups

  • Fixes when it's real: add a fillet, move the hole or feature, add material locally.
  • Fixes when it's an artifact: model the real fillet, spread the load over a realistic area, use a remote/distributed constraint, or read stress a short distance away (Saint-Venant).
  • Best proof: a strain gauge at that spot during testing.

cards.q: You need 1,000 of one of your suspension parts in a month. How does your design change? What if it's in production for years?
cards.a:
Short run: cut setups and tools, because setups take the most time. Design so it can be done on a 5-axis in one or two setups, use one corner radius so a single end mill does the whole part, standardize hole sizes, and use a fixture with hard stops so you're not re-indicating every part. Rough the profile on a waterjet or laser first so the CNC only does finish work.

Long run, years of production: switch to a near-net-shape process. Casting (or forging for strength), injection molding for plastic parts, stamping for sheet metal. Tooling is expensive up front, but per-part time and material waste drop dramatically, and the cost is spread over thousands of parts. Then only the critical features get machined.

Follow-ups

  • Casting and molding are basically the same idea: one for metal, one for plastic. You don't need to know every detail, just that they exist and when they pay off.
  • Forging gives better grain flow and fatigue strength than casting, which matters for suspension parts.
  • Design for the process: draft angles, uniform walls, and generous radii for casting and molding.

cards.q: How would you inspect those parts? What if inspection becomes the bottleneck?
cards.a:
Start from function: find the features that actually matter. On an upright or knuckle that's the bores for the press-fit spherical bearings and tapered roller bearings, plus hole positions that set the geometry. Do a full first-article inspection on a CMM, then check critical features on every part with fast gauges (go/no-go pin gauges, bore gauges) and reject anything out. Non-critical features get checked less often.

Once the process has shown it's consistent (every bore in tolerance for many batches), move from 100% inspection to statistical sampling: pull a random sample from each batch, and track the measurements on a control chart (SPC) so you catch drift before parts go out of tolerance. If a sample fails, go back to 100% and find the cause.

Follow-ups

  • Cpk measures process capability: how far the process is from the tolerance limits relative to its spread. Cpk ≥ 1.33 is a common bar for reducing inspection.
  • Safety-critical features may stay at 100% inspection no matter what.
  • Better: build checks into the process (in-machine probing, poka-yoke fixtures).

cards.q: A rocket with one engine. How much thrust does it need to hover? Two engines on opposite sides?
cards.a:
One engine: thrust = weight, T = mg. That's it; a simple first question is usually just simple. Two engines opposite each other with the center of gravity on the centerline: each provides mg/2.

If the CG is off-center, they're unequal: T₁ + T₂ = mg, and moments about the CG must balance, T₁·d₁ = T₂·d₂, so the engine closer to the CG pushes harder.

Follow-ups

  • The question gets harder from here; expect gimbals next.

cards.q: Now the single engine is on a gimbal. What changes if you tilt it?
cards.a:
(Our recording cut off here, so these are the likely follow-ups.) Tilt the thrust by θ: only T·cos θ holds the rocket up, so to keep hovering you need T = mg/cos θ. The sideways part, T·sin θ, pushes the rocket sideways and, because the engine is below the center of gravity, creates a moment T·sin θ·d about the CG, so the rocket starts to rotate. That's how gimbals steer: a small tilt makes a turning moment, the vehicle rotates, and then the main thrust points where you want to go. For a steady hover, the thrust line has to pass through the CG.

Follow-ups

  • As propellant burns, the CG moves, so the gimbal angle needed to keep the thrust through the CG changes during flight.
  • Engine-out with two engines: the remaining engine must gimbal so its thrust line passes through the CG, or the vehicle tumbles.

cards.q: A Christmas tree sits on a stand with three identical cantilevered legs. How do you reduce leg deflection, and where is the stress highest?
cards.a:
Each leg is a cantilever: δ = PL³/(3EI). To reduce deflection: shorten the legs (L³ is the big lever), increase I (taller section or an I-beam/tube), use a stiffer material (higher E), or reduce the load (a lighter tree). Along a leg, the bending moment is highest at the fixed end, so that's where the stress peaks. With identical legs and the tree centered, each leg carries a third of the weight.

Follow-ups

  • Interviewers mostly care that you know how the variables scale (L³, E, I), not the exact coefficient (3 for a cantilever, 48 for a simply supported center load).
  • For a tree that only pushes down, an I-beam leg oriented with its web vertical is the most mass-efficient.

cards.q: Swap one aluminum leg for steel (same geometry). How is the load shared now?
cards.a:
The answer the interviewer was looking for: the steel leg carries more. If the legs are all forced to deflect the same amount (the hub drops level), each leg's force is (3EI/L³)·δ, so with identical geometry the force is proportional to E. Steel (200 GPa) vs aluminum (70 GPa): steel takes about 59% and each aluminum leg about 21%, and the steel leg's stress is higher too because it carries more force on the same section. In the mock I said the force split stays even; the point of the question is that stiffer paths attract load when the deflections are tied together.

The catch worth saying out loud: three legs evenly spaced around a centered load is statically determinate. Three unknown leg forces, three equations (vertical force and moments about two axes), so statics alone gives W/3 per leg no matter the stiffness. The hub doesn't drop level; it tilts slightly toward the softer aluminum legs. Stiffness only decides the split when there are more supports than statics needs (four or more legs, legs in a line, or something holding the hub level).

Follow-ups

  • Best answer in an interview: give the stiffness answer, then add 'strictly, three symmetric legs are determinate, so each takes a third and the hub tilts; stiffness would matter with four legs or a level constraint.' That shows you understand both.
  • Stiffer load paths attract load in indeterminate structures. That's why you can't add a stiff part 'just for backup' without it taking over the load.
  • Same logic as the two concentric tubes (which are forced to stretch equally by rigid plates) and the hexagon table (six legs, indeterminate).

cards.q: The stand gets hot (not hot enough to change the heat treatment). How does the load split change?
cards.a:
The answer they want: the aluminum legs carry a bit less and the steel leg a bit more, because heat affects aluminum more. In the equal-deflection model that comes from stiffness: aluminum's modulus drops faster with temperature than steel's, so the aluminum legs get relatively softer.

On thermal expansion: aluminum grows about twice as much as steel (α ≈ 23 vs 12 ×10⁻⁶/°C). In the mock we reasoned that the longer legs get softer because L is cubed, but if a leg grows in every direction, I grows as size⁴ and L³ as size³, so k = 3EI/L³ actually goes up slightly, by about αΔT, a fraction of a percent. The bigger effect is that the legs end up different lengths. With three legs that's harmless: the hub just tilts and each leg still carries a third. With more legs, or legs fixed at both ends, the mismatch creates thermal stress, like the two-tube SpaceX question.

Follow-ups

  • Being able to say 'the geometric effect is actually tiny, and three legs are determinate anyway' shows you checked instead of guessing.
  • At much higher temperature, aluminum alloys lose strength quickly above about 150–200°C and the precipitation-hardened tempers overage, which is the heat-treatment point you raised.

cards.q: The tree goes in a busy mall where it gets kicked and bumped from every direction. What leg cross-section now?
cards.a:
A round tube (or a square tube). An I-beam is great for one known bending direction, but it's weak about its other axis and very weak in torsion, and kicks come from every direction and twist the leg. A closed round tube has the same stiffness in every bending direction and is by far the best in torsion for its weight.

Follow-ups

  • Closed sections beat open ones in torsion by hundreds of times (see the open vs closed tube card).
  • In the mock I reasoned about tension and compression; the stronger answer is about bending direction and torsion.

cards.q: Which way does a hot dog split, and why?
cards.a:
Lengthwise. It's a thin pressure vessel: hoop stress is pr/t and axial stress is pr/2t, so the hoop stress is twice as big. The hoop stress acts around the circumference, trying to pull the skin apart around the hot dog, and a crack opens perpendicular to the biggest tensile stress. A crack perpendicular to the hoop direction runs along the length.

Follow-ups

  • Common confusion (it got me in the mock): the stress direction and the crack direction are perpendicular. Hoop stress is circumferential, so the crack is axial.
  • Same reason pipes, tanks, and soda cans split lengthwise, and why longitudinal welds on pressure vessels are more critical.
  • Derive it: cut the cylinder lengthwise, σ·2tL = p·2rL gives pr/t; cut it across, σ·2πrt = p·πr² gives pr/2t.

subs.title: Problem Set: Wheel Bolts and Lug Nuts

cards.q: Fully threaded, partially threaded, or shoulder bolt, all the same nominal size. Rank them in tension, and where is the stress highest?
cards.a:
In tension, every bolt fails at its smallest, sharpest section. Fully and partially threaded: at the thread roots, usually at the first engaged thread at the nut face, where most of the load transfers. Their static tensile strength is about the same, set by the thread's tensile stress area. Partially threaded is still the better bolt: there are no thread notches along the grip, so the only notches are in the engaged threads, and a smooth shank can sit in a shear plane.

The shoulder bolt is the weakest in tension. Its threaded end is a size smaller than the shoulder, and there's an undercut (neck) where the shoulder steps down to the thread: a small diameter plus a sharp change in section is a big stress concentration, and that's where it breaks. Ranking: partially threaded ≥ fully threaded > shoulder.

Follow-ups

  • Shoulder bolts are for locating and for pivots in shear, not for clamping loads.
  • In the mock I ranked the shoulder bolt first because of its bigger shank. The trap: a chain is only as strong as its smallest link, and the shoulder bolt's smallest link is its thread and undercut.
  • Sharp corners concentrate stress, which is why thread roots and undercuts are where bolts fail, and why rolled threads and fillets help.

cards.q: Now the bolts are in shear (driving, the wheel loads the hub sideways). Rank them.
cards.a:
Shoulder bolt first: its precision-ground shoulder sits in the shear plane with a tight fit, so the full diameter carries shear and the parts can't slip. Partially threaded second: the full-diameter smooth shank is in the shear plane. Fully threaded last: the shear plane cuts through the threads, so only the minor diameter carries it, and the thread roots are notches. Never put threads in shear.

Follow-ups

  • That's why nearly all suspension bolts on the Baja car are partially threaded, with the grip length chosen so the shank spans the shear planes. Worth checking the upright camber link bolts.
  • Even better: enough preload that friction carries the shear and the bolt never sees it.

cards.q: You torque four lug nuts with a torque wrench. How do you torque them relative to each other? Then you lose one off a bridge.
cards.a:
Evenly: all four to the same spec, in a star (crisscross) pattern, in two or three passes, so the wheel seats flat and the preload is even. With only three nuts, both answers can be defended if you justify them: torque to the same spec (the spec already has a big safety factor, and over-torquing could yield the studs), or torque a bit higher to recover total clamp force (bolts usually have margin). What matters is the reasoning: preload is what holds the wheel on.

Follow-ups

  • Then drive slowly and replace the nut soon. Three evenly spaced nuts still locate the wheel.

cards.q: The rim face under one nut is scratched, so there's more friction there. Torque more, less, or the same?
cards.a:
More. What holds the wheel to the hub is the bolt's preload (clamp force), not the friction under the nut. Torque = K·D·P, and K is mostly friction. More friction under the nut means the torque wrench clicks before the stud has stretched as much, so the same torque gives less preload on that stud. To get the same clamp force, you need more torque (or better, clean up the surface or replace the part so the friction matches the spec).

Follow-ups

  • Most people say less, thinking friction helps hold the parts together. Friction under the nut actually fights the bolt stretching.
  • This is why lubrication changes the torque spec: less friction, more preload for the same torque, so lubricated specs are lower.

cards.q: You drop a second lug nut. Now what?
cards.a: Borrow one nut from each of the other wheels. Every wheel ends up with three nuts, spread evenly around the hub, which is safe to drive slowly to a shop. Better than leaving one wheel with only two.

cards.q: A block sits on two springs with the same shape, but spring A is stiffer than spring B. Which one takes more load?
cards.a:
Spring A. If the block is rigid and sits level, both springs compress the same amount, so each force is F = kδ and the load splits in proportion to stiffness: F_A / F_B = k_A / k_B. This is the same idea as the three-legged table: parallel load paths share load by stiffness, not equally.

Follow-ups

  • Same question with beams: a block resting on an aluminum beam and a steel beam of identical geometry. The steel beam is about 3 times stiffer, so it carries about 3/4 of the load and the aluminum beam about 1/4.
  • If the block can tilt or the load is off-center, the split changes. Say that assumption out loud.

cards.q: Define strength vs. stiffness in your own words.
cards.a:
Stiffness is how much something resists deforming: how much it bends, stretches, or compresses under a load. It depends on the material's modulus E and the geometry (A, I, length). Strength is how much stress it can take before it yields or breaks. Short version: stiff means hard to deform, strong means hard to break.

Follow-ups

  • Stiff but not strong: glass and ceramics barely deflect, then shatter.
  • Strong but not very stiff: high-strength aluminum like 7075 can out-yield mild steel, but its modulus is still about one third of steel's, so it deflects about 3 times as much.
  • Common trap: heat treating or picking a stronger alloy of the same metal raises strength but barely changes stiffness. E for almost every steel is about 200 GPa.

cards.q: Explain the stress-strain curve.
cards.a:
It comes from a tensile test. Walk the curve left to right:

  1. Linear elastic region: stress is proportional to strain up to the proportional limit (P). The slope is Young's modulus, E = σ/ε.
  2. Elastic limit (E): the highest stress with no permanent deformation.
  3. Yield point (Y): where plastic deformation starts. For metals without a sharp yield, use the 0.2% offset method.
  4. Strain hardening: past yield, stress keeps rising as the material plastically deforms.
  5. Ultimate tensile strength (U): the peak of the curve. After this the specimen necks.
  6. Fracture (F): the specimen breaks.

If you unload from the plastic region, the material comes back down along a line parallel to the original elastic slope.
