Use worst case for low volume or critical fits, and RSS for high-volume production with many parts in the stack.

cards.q: How do you figure out the load cases for a new design?
cards.a:
Walk through the part's whole life and ask what pushes on it, then trace each load from where it enters to where it leaves (the load path to ground). The buckets I use: normal operating loads, peak or impact loads, loads from the environment and other machines, handling and drop loads, passive loads that are always there (gravity, preload, belt tension, spinning mass), thermal loads, and repeated loads that drive fatigue.

For a combat robot that's: weapon spin-up (torsion, belt tension, friction, motor heat), weapon impact (torque shock, shaft and hub shear, huge bearing loads), getting hit by the opponent (local impact, shock through the chassis), hitting walls and the floor, and passive loads (weight on the baseplate, constant spinning, electronics heat). Then size every part on the path against its worst case.

Follow-ups

  • Quick sanity test from the lecture: if you wouldn't pick the robot up to waist height and drop it in any orientation, find out why and fix it. Real parts get dropped, shipped, and mishandled.
  • Parts out of a weapon's reach still get hit when the machine hits a wall or lands, so every joint needs to share load with the whole structure.
  • Same thinking for any product: list the cases, find the governing one for each part, and don't forget assembly and transport loads.

cards.q: How do you protect a drivetrain from shock loads?
cards.a:
Decide what fails first, on purpose. Put a mechanical fuse in the load path: the cheapest, easiest-to-replace element should slip or break before anything expensive does. In a belt-driven weapon, size it so the belt slips before the motor shaft or weapon shaft twists. Other fuses: shear pins, slip clutches, torque limiters, and compliant couplings.

Transmission choice sets how much shock reaches the motor. From most slip (most protection) to least: rubber band, round belt, V-belt, timing belt, chain and sprocket, then gears. A stiff positive drive like a chain or gearbox sends the full impact back into the motor and its bearings.

Follow-ups

  • The fuse has to be predictable: a belt that slips at a known torque is a fuse; a shaft that might crack somewhere is not.
  • Snowblowers use shear pins on the auger for the same reason: a rock should break a $1 pin, not the gearbox.
  • Tradeoff: slip wastes energy and makes heat, so belts need ventilation and the right power rating.

cards.q: Belt vs chain vs gears: how do you choose, and what loads does a belt put on the shafts?
cards.a:
Belts: quiet, light, cheap, tolerate misalignment, absorb shock, and can slip (timing belts don't slip but still have some compliance). They need tension and have lower power density. Chains: compact, high torque, long center distances, no slip, but they need lubrication, stretch over time, and transmit shock. Gears: most compact, highest efficiency and precision, but need accurate center distances, transmit full shock, and cost more.

Belt tension is a load that's always there. The tight side and slack side both pull the pulleys toward each other, so each shaft sees a radial load of roughly T_tight + T_slack (the vector sum, so slightly less when the spans aren't parallel), even with no torque being transmitted. That loads shafts, fasteners, and bearings on the tensioner too.

Follow-ups

  • Real failure from the club: a belt tensioner hub sheared from belt tension alone. The tensioner is a small part carrying the full belt load, so check it.
  • Motor shafts are usually small and long, so belt tension puts them in bending right at the bearing. Keep the pulley close to the motor face.
  • Torque transmitted = (T_tight − T_slack) × pulley radius.

cards.q: How do you choose a bearing?
cards.a:
Start from the loads: radial (perpendicular to the shaft), axial or thrust (along it), or both, plus speed and shock. Ball bearings handle moderate radial and some axial load at high speed. Roller and needle bearings carry much higher radial loads in a small package (line contact instead of point contact), which is why needle rollers are a good choice for weapon impacts. Tapered rollers or angular-contact bearings handle combined radial and thrust. Bushings (plain bearings) are cheap, compact, and shock-tolerant, but have more friction and wear.

Then check ratings: the static load rating C₀ for shock and heavy loads at low speed (it guards against denting the races, called brinelling), and the dynamic rating C for life: L₁₀ = (C/P)^p million revolutions, with p = 3 for ball bearings and 10/3 for rollers. L₁₀ is the life 90% of bearings reach.

Follow-ups

  • Double the load and a ball bearing's life drops by 8× (2³).
  • Also check speed limits, sealing (dirt and water), and fits (press fit on the rotating ring).
  • Use two bearings spread apart to resist moment loads; one bearing is a pivot.

cards.q: Live shaft vs dead shaft: what's the difference and when do you use each?
cards.a:
Live shaft: the shaft spins with the wheel or weapon, sits in bearings mounted in the frame, and carries torque plus bending. Dead shaft: the shaft is fixed to the frame and doesn't rotate; the bearings are inside the wheel or weapon hub, which spins around it. A dead shaft only sees bending and shear (no torsion or fatigue from rotation), can double as a structural member that ties the frame together, and is easier to make stiff. Torque is delivered by a pulley or sprocket bolted directly to the hub.

Follow-ups

  • Many spinning weapons use dead shafts: the shaft becomes part of the frame, and the hub and bearings take the hits.
  • Live shafts make sense when you need to take torque off the shaft somewhere else, like a drive axle feeding two wheels.
  • A rotating shaft in bending sees fully reversed stress every revolution, which is a fatigue load; a dead shaft doesn't.

cards.q: How should you support a wheel shaft, and why shouldn't the wheel hang directly on the motor shaft?
cards.a:
Support the shaft on both sides of the wheel (simply supported) rather than overhanging it off one side (a cantilever). For the same span and load, a simply supported shaft with a center load sees a peak moment of PL/4, while a cantilever sees PL: four times lower bending, and much less deflection.

Keep impact loads off the motor's own shaft. Mount the wheel on its own shaft and bearings and drive it through a belt, gear, or coupling (indirect mounting). If a landing bends or shifts the motor shaft, the rotor can hit the magnets, which crack and destroy the motor permanently.

Follow-ups

  • Same principle in industry: put pulleys and gears between bearings, not overhung, or keep the overhang short.
  • Couplings that allow a little misalignment protect the motor from frame flex.

cards.q: Why does a small imbalance in a spinning part matter at high RPM?
cards.a:
An off-center mass m at radius e creates a rotating force F = m·e·ω², and ω is squared. A 1 g imbalance 50 mm from the axis at 10,000 rpm (about 1,050 rad/s) creates about 55 N, sweeping around once per revolution. That's a cyclic load on the shaft and bearings 10,000 times a minute: vibration, bearing wear, loosened fasteners, and fatigue. At 20,000 rpm it's four times as much.

Follow-ups

  • Fix: balance the part (statically and dynamically), machine it symmetric, and check that teeth or blades are evenly spaced and equal mass.
  • Include centrifugal stress in the safety-factor calc for any spinning mass; it often needs its own FEA study.
  • If the spin speed hits the shaft's critical speed (its bending natural frequency), the imbalance response grows huge.

cards.q: Why do motors overheat near stall, and how should you size one?
cards.a:
In a DC motor, torque is proportional to current, and heat is I²R. At stall the motor draws its maximum current (only resistance limits it, since there's no back-EMF), so it makes the most heat while producing zero mechanical power, and at low speed its own fan moves the least air. Running near stall torque means peak heating for longer.

So size the motor so normal operation is well below its stall torque, ideally near its peak-efficiency speed, and give it airflow. Don't enclose motors, ESCs, or batteries in a sealed box: every spin-up and hard maneuver adds heat with nowhere to go.

Follow-ups

  • Peak mechanical power is at half the no-load speed and half the stall torque; peak efficiency is at higher speed and lower torque.
  • A gear reduction lets a smaller motor run at higher, cooler speed for the same output torque.
  • Heat paths: conduction to a metal chassis or heat sink, plus airflow.

cards.q: How do you design a bolted interface so the bolts don't carry shear?
cards.a:
Let geometry carry the shear and use the bolts to clamp. Options: tabs and slots or pockets that interlock, a shoulder or step that the part bears against, dowel pins for location and shear, or enough bolt preload that friction carries the load. Bolts in direct shear are a weak, loosening-prone path, especially through thin plates.

Thin plates with small fasteners also fail by bearing (the hole elongates as the plate behind the bolt crushes) or tear-out (the material between the hole and the edge shears out). Shoulder bolts, bushings, or spacers put a bigger diameter through the plate to lower bearing stress, and keeping enough edge distance stops tear-out; for a given force you can solve for the minimum edge distance.

Follow-ups

  • A little bearing deformation can actually help by work-hardening the hole, but don't design on it.
  • Watch for stress concentrations at interfaces, where the load path changes direction.
  • Same idea as a slip-critical joint: preload plus friction means the bolt never sees shear.

cards.q: A part is plenty strong. Why might it still need to be stiffer?
cards.a:
Because deflection can break the function without breaking the part. Example from combat robotics: if the wheels mount to the baseplate and the robot's weight bends the baseplate, the wheels camber and you lose traction. Other examples: gear centers moving apart under load (bad mesh, tooth wear), a seal losing compression, a bearing bore going out of line, or an optical or measurement mount drifting.

Follow-ups

  • Stiffness comes from E and geometry (EI, AE), not strength, so a stronger material doesn't fix it.
  • Check the deflection that matters to the function, not just the stress against yield.

cards.q: Hard vs tough: how do you pick a material for a wear or impact surface?
cards.a:
Hard materials (high-carbon or hardened steels) resist wear and keep an edge, but they're brittle and can crack or shatter under impact. Tough materials absorb energy by deforming. For armor, it needs to be either so hard the opponent can't damage it, or ductile enough that it tears instead of cracking, and thick enough to lose some material and still work. Many designs use a tough core with a hard surface (case hardening) to get both.

Follow-ups

  • Don't machine razor-sharp teeth on an impact weapon: they round off after the first hits anyway, so starting blunt makes the performance predictable.
  • Design for the worn state, not the new one.
  • Tool steels like S7 are popular for impact parts because they balance hardness and toughness.

cards.q: How would you select the material for a specific mechanical component?
cards.a:
1. Define the function and environment: What loads (static, cyclic, impact)? What temperatures? Corrosion, chemicals, moisture, or seawater? Wear? Weight and cost limits?
  2. Pick candidates with the right properties: use tools like MatWeb or Ashby charts. Cyclic or high loads point to yield strength, hardness, and fatigue resistance. High temperature points to heat resistance and thermal expansion. Weight-critical parts point to aluminum, titanium, or composites, compared on strength-to-weight (σ/ρ) or stiffness-to-weight (E/ρ).
  3. Check manufacturability: Can it be machined, welded, cast, or forged? Does it need heat treatment? Can it be joined to the parts around it? Does it need to meet a standard like ASTM or ISO?

Follow-ups

  • Give a quick example from your own work, such as why the Baja A-arms are steel tube, or why 3D-printed parts were fine for the centerlock testbench but not for the vehicle.

cards.q: Compare steel and aluminum.
cards.a:
Aluminum is about one third the density of steel (about 2.7 vs 7.85 g/cm³) and about one third the stiffness (E ≈ 70 vs 200 GPa). It's good when mass matters, conducts heat much better, and resists corrosion through its oxide layer. Steel holds its strength at much higher temperatures, has better fatigue behavior, wears better, and is usually cheaper and easier to weld. I'd pick aluminum for weight-sensitive structures at moderate temperature, and steel for high-load, high-temperature, wear, or stiffness-critical parts, depending on the load case and environment.

Follow-ups

  • Interesting fact: steel and aluminum have almost the same stiffness-to-weight ratio (E/ρ). For the same mass, an aluminum part can be thicker and end up just as stiff, which is why aluminum works so well for thin-walled structures.
  • Fatigue: most steels have an endurance limit (below a certain stress they last indefinitely). Aluminum doesn't, so it eventually fails under any cyclic load given enough cycles.
  • Aluminum loses a lot of strength in the heat-affected zone when welded, especially heat-treated alloys like 6061-T6.

cards.q: You have two identical-looking blocks, one steel and one aluminum. How do you tell them apart?
cards.a:
• Weigh them: steel is about 3 times heavier for the same volume. Fastest and most reliable.
  • Magnet: most steels are magnetic. Trap: austenitic stainless steels (like 304) are barely magnetic, so a magnet alone can fool you.
  • Hardness: steel is usually harder, so aluminum scratches or dents more easily.
  • Thermal conductivity: aluminum feels colder to the touch and heats up faster from one end.
  • Sound: tap them; steel rings at a different pitch.

Melting or corroding them works in principle, but it's destructive, so mention it last if at all.

cards.q: Rank the coefficients of thermal expansion of aluminum, bronze, and steel.
cards.a: Aluminum (about 23 × 10⁻⁶ /K) > bronze (about 18) > steel (about 12). For reference, copper is about 17 and titanium about 8.6.

cards.q: How do ductile and brittle materials fail?
cards.a: Ductile materials yield and fail in shear along slip planes, about 45° to the load, with necking and a cup-and-cone fracture, so there's plenty of warning. Brittle materials fail in tension, perpendicular to the largest principal stress, starting at a flaw, suddenly. Brittle materials like concrete, cast iron, and ceramics are much stronger in compression than tension.

cards.q: Typical property values
cards.a:
• Mild steel (A36): E ≈ 200 GPa, yield ≈ 250 MPa, UTS ≈ 400 to 550 MPa.
  • 4130 chromoly (Baja frame tubing): yield ≈ 435 MPa normalized, UTS ≈ 670 MPa.
  • Aluminum 6061-T6: E ≈ 69 GPa, yield ≈ 276 MPa, UTS ≈ 310 MPa.
  • Aluminum 7075-T6: yield ≈ 500 MPa, UTS ≈ 570 MPa.

cards.q: What do annealing, normalizing, quenching, and tempering do?
cards.a:
• Annealing: heat above the critical temperature, then cool slowly in the furnace. Softer, more ductile, stress-relieved, easier to machine.
  • Normalizing: heat above critical, then cool in air. Finer, more uniform grain, a bit stronger than annealed.
  • Quenching: cool rapidly in water or oil to form martensite. Very hard and strong but brittle.
  • Tempering: reheat a quenched part below critical. Gives up some hardness for much better toughness.
  • Stress relief: heat below critical and cool slowly to remove residual stress without changing the structure much.

None of these change Young's modulus. Forged parts are heat treated to relieve residual stress, refine and even out the grain structure, improve machinability, and hit the required hardness and strength.

cards.q: What are the ways to strengthen a metal?
cards.a:
• Grain size reduction: grain boundaries block dislocation motion, so finer grains mean higher strength and toughness (Hall-Petch).
  • Solid solution strengthening: alloying atoms distort the lattice and pin dislocations.
  • Strain hardening (cold work): plastic deformation multiplies dislocations, which tangle and resist further slip.
  • Precipitation hardening: fine particles block dislocations (the T6 in 6061-T6).
  • Heat treatment: quench and temper for martensite.

cards.q: What are the main types of steel?
cards.a:
• Low carbon (under ~0.3% C): ductile, very weldable, barely responds to heat treatment.
  • Medium carbon (~0.3 to 0.6% C): heat treatable, stronger but less ductile. Shafts, gears, axles.
  • High carbon (over ~0.6% C): hardest and strongest, least ductile. Springs and tools.
  • Stainless: at least about 10.5% chromium for corrosion resistance. Austenitic grades like 304 are nonmagnetic; 17-4 PH is precipitation hardened.

AISI/SAE four-digit codes: the first two digits give the alloy family and the last two give carbon in hundredths of a percent. 4130 is chromium-molybdenum steel with 0.30% carbon.

cards.q: What mechanical tests should you know?
cards.a:
• Tensile test: pull a specimen at a set rate to get the stress-strain curve.
  • Bend test: three-point bend to a set angle; a quick check of ductility and weld soundness.
  • Charpy impact: a pendulum breaks a notched bar; the energy absorbed measures toughness and shows the ductile-to-brittle transition temperature.
  • Fracture toughness (CTOD, K_IC): load a pre-cracked specimen to see how much a crack can take.
  • Hardness (Rockwell, Brinell, Vickers): resistance to indentation; it correlates roughly with tensile strength.

cards.q: How does carbon fiber carry load?
cards.a: The fibers carry tension along their length; the epoxy matrix holds them in place, transfers load between fibers, keeps them from buckling in compression, and carries shear. Align fibers with the load paths, and use a quasi-isotropic layup (0/±45/90) when loads come from several directions. Weak spots are interlaminar shear, impact damage, and bolted joints.

cards.q: You find a defect in a carbon fiber panel bonded to a foam core: about 0.010 in deep and the size of your pinky. It's for a crewed spacecraft module. How do you decide whether it's still flight-safe?
cards.a:
1. Stop and document it with a nonconformance report. Don't decide alone.
  2. Find the real extent with nondestructive inspection: visual, tap test, ultrasonic or thermography. The visible mark may hide a larger delamination or a disbond from the core.
  3. Compare it with the drawing's allowable defect criteria and the damage tolerance requirements.
  4. Analyze it: what load runs through that area, and what is the margin of safety with the defect modeled (a strength knockdown)? Crewed hardware has strict fracture control rules.
  5. Disposition through the review board with structures and quality: use as is with analysis, repair with an approved process (for example a scarf repair) and re-inspect, or scrap.
  6. Find the root cause so it doesn't happen again.

cards.q: Why would you use casting instead of CNC machining?
cards.a: Casting wins for complex shapes, internal cavities, large parts, and high volume, where the tooling cost spreads out and less material is wasted. CNC wins for low volume, tight tolerances, better material properties (wrought stock instead of cast), and fast design changes with no tooling. A common approach is to cast near net shape and then machine the critical features.

subs.title: Sheet Metal, Casting, Molding, and Additive

cards.q: Sand casting vs die casting
cards.a: Sand casting is cheap for low quantities and can make very large parts, but it's less dimensionally accurate and has a rougher finish. Die casting pushes molten metal into a steel die: good tolerances and finish, little post-machining, and high volume, but the tooling is expensive, part size is limited, and porosity makes guaranteed mechanical properties harder. Your source notes listed tight tolerances as a general casting advantage; that's true for die and investment casting, not sand casting.

cards.q: Name the main parts of an injection molding machine, and the key design rules for molded parts.
cards.a:
Machine: hopper, barrel with heater bands, reciprocating screw, nozzle, the mold (cavity half and core half with runners and gates), the clamping unit with tie bars, and ejector pins.

  • Keep wall thickness uniform. Too thick causes sink marks and long cycle times; too thin causes short shots.
  • Add draft, usually 1 to 2 degrees (more with textured surfaces), so parts eject cleanly.
  • Use radii instead of sharp corners, and ribs instead of thick sections (rib thickness about 50 to 60% of the wall).
  • Avoid undercuts, or plan for slides and lifters.
  • Common defects and fixes: sink marks (thinner sections, more packing pressure or hold time), short shots (more fill pressure or thicker walls), flash (too much pressure or a worn mold), warping, and weld lines.

cards.q: Hot runner vs cold runner molds
cards.a: Hot runners keep the plastic molten up to the gate: less waste, faster cycles, better part quality, but higher cost and more maintenance. Cold runners are cheaper and simpler and suit heat-sensitive materials, but the runner is scrap every shot and cycles are slower.

cards.q: Compare the main 3D printing processes.
cards.a:
• FDM: filament through a heated nozzle. Cheap and fast, but weak between layers.
  • Vat polymerization (SLA, DLP, MSLA): light cures liquid resin. SLA uses a laser, DLP a projector, MSLA an LCD-masked UV array. Fine detail and smooth surfaces.
  • SLS and MJF: polymer powder bed fused by a laser (SLS) or by inkjet agent plus infrared heat (MJF). Strong nylon parts with no supports.
  • SLM / DMLS: a laser fully melts metal powder. Dense metal parts with complex geometry.
  • WAAM / DED: an arc or laser deposits weld wire layer by layer. Large metal parts quickly, but rough and needs machining.

cards.q: You're printing with wire-arc additive (WAAM) and find a hole in a section that's already printed. What do you do?
cards.a:
1. Treat it as a defect: stop, document it, and find its full extent with CT, ultrasonic, or X-ray.
  2. Grind or machine the void out back to sound metal.
  3. Re-deposit weld to fill it, controlling interpass temperature and shielding gas.
  4. Stress relieve, finish machine, and re-inspect (dye penetrant or X-ray).
  5. Find the root cause, such as contamination, shielding gas problems, or bad parameters.

cards.q: You have 24 hours to build a box that will be judged on strength and squareness. What do you do?
cards.a:
1. Pick a material you can work fast and accurately, like plywood or aluminum angle.
  2. Spend the first hour on a sketch and cut list.
  3. Get squareness from fixturing: cut with stops so matching pieces are identical, assemble against a square jig, and check that both diagonals match.
  4. Get strength from the joints: rabbet or dado joints with glue and screws, plus corner blocks or gussets. A glued back panel acts as a shear web and stiffens the box against racking.
  5. Glue up, clamp, and let it cure overnight.

cards.q: How would you design an ice cube for optimal manufacturing?
cards.a: Open-ended, so define "optimal" first. For fast freezing, maximize surface area to volume with thin shapes. For easy release, add draft and use a flexible silicone tray with rounded corners. To avoid cracking, keep the thickness uniform. For drinks, larger cubes with low surface area melt slower. Name the tradeoff out loud: fast freezing and slow melting pull in opposite directions.

cards.q: Describe how a forklift works.
cards.a: Hydraulic cylinders raise a carriage on a telescoping mast. A chain runs over a sheave on top of the cylinder, so the forks move twice as far as the cylinder stroke. Tilt cylinders angle the mast back to cradle the load. A heavy counterweight at the rear keeps the combined center of gravity inside the stability triangle formed by the front wheels and the rear pivot. Rear-wheel steering gives a tight turning radius. Rated capacity drops as the load center moves farther out, because the tipping moment about the front axle grows.

cards.q: How would you determine the impact forces on a component you designed for a race car?
cards.a: Start with energy: F_avg = KE/δ, where δ is how far the structure deflects while absorbing the energy, or use impulse-momentum, F = mΔv/Δt. Use measured accelerations from data logging if you have them, otherwise standard load cases (for example a multiple-g bump, braking, and cornering) times a dynamic factor. Then confirm with FEA and, ideally, a test. This is exactly what your Baja load case analysis does.

cards.q: A pack is wired 10S1P or 5S2P from the same cells. Which gets hotter?
cards.a: Heat in each cell is I_cell² × R_internal. Cells in parallel split the current. If both packs deliver the same current, the 5S2P cells each carry half of it and make a quarter of the heat, so the 10S1P pack runs hotter. If both deliver the same power, the 5S2P pack has half the voltage, so it needs twice the current; each parallel cell then carries the same current as a 10S1P cell, and the heating per cell comes out the same. State the assumption, then reason it through.

cards.q: What changes the resistance of a section of wire?
cards.a: R = ρL/A: the material's resistivity, the length, and the cross-sectional area. Temperature matters too: metals get more resistive as they heat up. At high AC frequencies the skin effect raises resistance, and connections add contact resistance. The heat generated is P = I²R, so the energy over time is I²Rt.

cards.q: When sizing an electrical wire, what matters?
cards.a:
• Current (ampacity) and the allowable temperature rise for the insulation.
  • Voltage drop over the run length, which matters most at low voltage (that's why USB cable size is limited by current and voltage drop at 5 V).
  • Ambient temperature and how many wires are bundled together.
  • Mechanical needs like flexibility and strain relief, and a fuse sized to protect the wire.

cards.q: Where would you put fuses in a battery pack, and why?
cards.a: A main fuse as close to the pack's positive terminal as possible, so the entire run of wire downstream is protected from a short. In packs with cells in parallel, add cell-level fuses (fuse wires) so a single shorted cell can't have its neighbors dump current into it. Rate fuses above the normal operating current, below the wire's ampacity, and for DC at the pack voltage.

cards.q: AC vs DC power
cards.a: AC can be stepped up and down easily with transformers, so the grid transmits at high voltage and low current to cut I²R losses. Homes in the US get AC at 120/240 V, 60 Hz. DC comes from batteries and solar and powers electronics and EVs; very long transmission lines sometimes use high-voltage DC.

cards.q: Quick definitions
cards.a:
• Capacitor: stores charge and resists changes in voltage.
  • Inductor: stores energy in a magnetic field and resists changes in current. A transformer is two coupled inductors.
  • Diode: lets current flow one way only; used to turn AC into DC.
  • Transistor / MOSFET: a switch or amplifier controlled by a small signal at the gate or base.
  • Op-amp: high-gain amplifier of the voltage difference between its two inputs; with feedback it builds amplifiers, filters, and comparators.
  • Voltage divider: two resistors in series; V_out = V_in · R₂/(R₁ + R₂).
  • Wheatstone bridge: measures small resistance changes; it's how strain gauges and many pressure transducers work.

cards.q: Thermocouple vs RTD vs thermistor
cards.a:
• Thermocouple: two different metals joined; the junction makes a voltage that depends on temperature. Rugged, cheap, and covers a huge temperature range, but less accurate.
  • RTD: a metal (usually platinum) whose resistance rises with temperature. Accurate and stable.
  • Thermistor: a ceramic resistor whose resistance usually drops with temperature. Very sensitive and cheap, but only over a narrow range.

cards.q: How do accelerometers and gyroscopes work?
cards.a: A MEMS accelerometer has a tiny proof mass on springs; acceleration moves the mass and the change in capacitance is measured. A MEMS gyroscope has a vibrating structure; rotation creates a Coriolis force on it, which is measured to get angular rate.

subs.title: FEA Setup: Mesh, Boundary Conditions, Loads

cards.q: How do you check if your FEA mesh is good?
cards.a:
• Run a mesh convergence study: refine until the peak stress in your area of interest changes by only a few percent.
  • Check element quality: aspect ratio, skewness, and Jacobian.
  • Refine locally at fillets, holes, and contact areas instead of everywhere.
  • Use quadratic elements (for example 10-node tets) for stress results.
  • Compare against a hand calculation.

cards.q: How do you know your FEA results are right?
cards.a:
• Hand calcs first: check the result against a simple estimate (a beam, a pressure vessel, σ = Mc/I) to make sure it's the right order of magnitude.
  • Mesh convergence: refine the mesh in the high-stress areas until the peak stress stops changing much.
  • Boundary conditions: fixed supports are stiffer than real ones and create fake stress peaks at the constraints. Make sure loads and supports match reality.
  • Singularities: stress at a sharp corner or point load keeps rising as you refine the mesh. That's a model artifact, not a real number.
  • Test: compare against physical tests or strain gauges where possible.

Follow-ups

  • Tie it to SKULL CRUSHER: ANSYS showed the critical areas near the bore and attachment points, which drove the fillet and thickness changes.

cards.q: Why do hand calculations still matter if you have FEA?
cards.a:
FEA is a numerical approximation: it chops the part into simple elements, approximates the physics on each, and patches them together. What comes out depends entirely on what goes in: geometry, material properties, loads, and boundary conditions. Simple hand models are how you choose the right FEA model, check that the inputs make sense, catch errors in the output, and actually understand why the part behaves the way it does.

Follow-ups

  • Refining the mesh makes results more accurate but run time grows quickly. A hand calc tells you when a result is already close enough.
  • Common mistakes hand calcs catch: wrong units (Pa vs MPa, mm vs m), over-constrained boundary conditions, loads applied at the wrong place, and stress singularities at sharp corners.
  • Good habit: before running the model, write down the stress and deflection you expect from a beam or plate formula.

sections.title: Open-Ended Design Questions
sections.intro: For these, the interviewer cares about your process more than the final answer. Clarify requirements, state assumptions, identify the main loads and failure modes, then size and choose materials.

cards.q: Design a hammock.
cards.a:
Start with requirements: maximum user weight, span between anchors, environment, and safety factor. Structurally, a hammock acts like a cable in tension, so anchor loads depend heavily on the hang angle. A tight, flat hammock creates huge anchor forces, so design for a reasonable sag (a hang angle around 30 degrees is common). Use a strong woven fabric such as ripstop nylon with reinforced edges. Size the end connections and straps for the full tension with a solid margin, and design them to resist fatigue, abrasion, and UV degradation. Make the anchor interface spread the load and adjust for different setups.

Follow-ups

  • Quick check: tension in each strap is T = W / (2 sin θ), where θ is the strap angle from horizontal. At 30 degrees, T equals the full body weight. Near horizontal, T shoots toward infinity.

cards.q: How would you get from the roof of one building to another, then down to the ground?
cards.a:
I'd use a portable rope access system. Anchor a static rope to a solid structural point on the first building, get the rope across the gap, secure it to the second building, and tension it into a Tyrolean traverse. Cross using a harness and pulley with a redundant safety line. On the second roof, use a separately anchored rope to rappel down. The key considerations are anchor strength, redundancy, rope tension, and edge protection so the rope doesn't get cut on the roof edge.

Follow-ups

  • Tension trap: a tight horizontal rope with a person hanging in the middle sees a tension many times their body weight, same math as the hammock.

cards.q: You're on a bridge and all the lug nuts fall off one wheel. How do you fix it?
cards.a: Take one lug nut from each of the other three wheels and put them on the bare wheel, so every wheel has at least three nuts. Drive slowly to the nearest shop. The point of the question is calm, practical problem solving with what you have.

sections.title: Quick-Reference Formula Sheet
sections.intro: Equations worth knowing cold. The sections below "Core equations" are a friend's two-page hand-calc cheat sheet (structures, dynamics, fluids, gas dynamics, rockets, orbits), typeset and checked. Anything I'd correct is flagged in the last card and noted where it appears.

cards.q: Mechanics of materials
cards.a:
• Stress and strain: σ = F/A, ε = ΔL/L, σ = Eε
  • Axial stiffness: k = EA/L. Deflection: δ = FL/(AE)
  • Bending stress: σ = Mc/I = M/S
  • Rectangle: I = bh³/12. Solid circle: I = πR⁴/4. Tube: I = π(Ro⁴ − Ri⁴)/4
  • Cantilever, end load: M_max = PL, δ = PL³/(3EI)
  • Simply supported, center load: M_max = PL/4, δ = PL³/(48EI)
  • Torsion: τ = Tr/J, θ = TL/(GJ), J = πR⁴/2 for a solid shaft
  • Euler buckling: P_cr = π²EI/(KL)²
  • Thin-walled pressure vessel: hoop σ = pr/t, axial σ = pr/(2t)
  • Factor of safety: FS = strength / working stress

cards.q: Dynamics, energy, power
cards.a:
• Kinetic energy: KE = ½mv². Rotational: ½Iω²
  • Work: W = F·d. Power: P = W/t = F·v = τω
  • Impulse-momentum: FΔt = mΔv
  • Natural frequency: ω_n = √(k/m)
  • Drag: F_D = ½ρC_D A V²

cards.q: Fluids and heat transfer
cards.a:
• Hydrostatic pressure: P = P_atm + ρgh
  • Ideal gas: PV = nRT (use Kelvin)
  • Mass flow: ṁ = ρAV
  • Steady momentum: ΣF = Σ(ṁV)_out − Σ(ṁV)_in
  • Bernoulli: P + ½ρV² + ρgh = constant
  • Conduction: q = −kA dT/dx. Convection: q = hAΔT. Radiation: q = εσA(T⁴ − T_surr⁴)
  • Thermal expansion: ΔL = αLΔT

cards.q: Material values
cards.a:
• Steel: E ≈ 200 GPa, ρ ≈ 7.85 g/cm³, α ≈ 12 × 10⁻⁶ /K, melts around 1400 to 1500°C
  • Aluminum: E ≈ 70 GPa, ρ ≈ 2.7 g/cm³, α ≈ 23 × 10⁻⁶ /K, melts around 660°C
  • Titanium (Ti-6Al-4V): E ≈ 114 GPa, ρ ≈ 4.4 g/cm³, α ≈ 8.6 × 10⁻⁶ /K, melts around 1600 to 1660°C

cards.q: Stress, strain, energy, and yield
cards.a:
• Hooke: σ = Eε, ε = ΔL/L, Poisson ν = −ε_lat/ε_long
  • True vs engineering: σ_true = σ_eng(1 + ε_eng), ε_true = ln(1 + ε_eng). They differ after necking starts.
  • Yield is usually defined at 0.2% offset (0.002 strain).
  • Von Mises: σ_vm = √{[(σ₁ − σ₂)² + (σ₂ − σ₃)² + (σ₃ − σ₁)²]/2}
  • Toughness = area under the whole σ-ε curve, ∫σ dε
  • Bar in tension: σ = F/A, ΔL = FL/(EA), a side dimension s shrinks by Δs = −ν·s·F/(EA), strain energy U = F²L/(2EA)
  • Shaft in torsion: τ = Tc/J, θ = TL/(GJ), G = E/(2(1 + ν))
  • Thermal: ε = αΔT, ΔL = LαΔT

Interview notes

  • Strain energy goes with F², so you can't add energies from separate loads; add the loads first.
  • Von Mises only uses differences of principal stresses, which is why hydrostatic pressure doesn't cause yield.

cards.q: Pins, bolts, lugs, and welds
cards.a:
Pin in shear (single shear; divide V by 2 for double shear):

  • Average: τ_avg = V/A_pin
  • Peak, solid round: τ_max = (4/3)·V/A. Thin hollow round: 2·V/A. Square: (3/2)·V/A.

Bolts:

  • Preload from torque: F = T/(K·D). K ≈ 0.10–0.15 lubricated, 0.15–0.20 dry.
  • Bolt stress: σ = (F_preload + external load beyond preload)/A_tensile. Until the joint separates, the bolt only sees a fraction of the external load.
  • Tensile stress area (standard): A_t = 0.7854·(D − 0.9743/n)², n = threads per inch. For ¼-20: 0.0318 in².
  • Thread pull-out: F ≈ 0.4·π·D·L_engaged·τ_ult (rough rule; about 40% of the thread cylinder is effectively in shear). If τ_ult isn't listed, use σ_ult/√3.

Lugs and plates:

  • Bearing: σ_br = F/(D·t), compared with the bearing allowable at your edge distance ratio e/D (often 1.5 or 2.0 in MMPDS). For a double clevis, each side carries F/2.
  • Shear tear-out: τ = F/(2·e·t), two shear planes from hole to edge (e = hole center to edge, conservative).

Fillet weld: τ ≈ V/(L·h/√2), throat = leg h × 0.707, compared with the weld shear allowable.

Interview notes

  • Never put threads in the shear plane (see the bolt cards).
  • Interviewers like hearing that the bolt mostly sees preload, not the external load, as long as the joint stays clamped.

cards.q: Beam deflection and max moment: the six cases
cards.a:
CaseMax deflection δMax moment
Cantilever, tip load FFL³/(3EI)FL (at the wall)
Cantilever, uniform load (total F)FL³/(8EI)FL/2
Simply supported, center load FFL³/(48EI)FL/4
Simply supported, uniform (total F)5FL³/(384EI)FL/8
Fixed-fixed, center load FFL³/(192EI)FL/8
Fixed-fixed, uniform (total F)FL³/(384EI)FL/12 (at the ends)

Bending stress σ = Mc/I. Cantilever stiffness k = 3EI/L³.

SectionI (bending)J (polar, round only)
Solid roundπR⁴/4 = πD⁴/64πR⁴/2 = πD⁴/32
Tubeπ(Ro⁴ − Ri⁴)/4π(Ro⁴ − Ri⁴)/2
Rectangle b × hbh³/12see note (not bh(b² + h²)/12 for torsion)

Interview notes

  • The coefficients (3, 8, 48, 192...) matter less than the scaling: deflection goes as L³ and 1/(EI). Fixing both ends makes a beam 4× stiffer than simply supporting it.
  • For a rectangle, bh(b² + h²)/12 is the polar moment of area, but it is NOT the torsion constant. Non-round sections warp, so use τ_max = T/(α·b·t²) and θ = TL/(β·b·t³·G) from a table (thin strip: α = β ≈ 1/3).

cards.q: Buckling
cards.a:
• Euler: F_cr = n·π²EI/L², with n = 1 pinned-pinned, about 2 pinned-fixed (2.05), 4 fixed-fixed, 0.25 fixed-free.
  • Equivalent to π²EI/(KL)² with K = 1, 0.7, 0.5, 2.
  • Stress form: σ_cr = π²E/(KL/r)², with r = √(I/A).

Interview notes

  • The sheet says Euler applies 'for L/R > 10'. That's too loose: Euler holds only for slender columns, where the slenderness ratio KL/r is above about √(2π²E/σ_y), around 126 for mild steel and ~70–100 for aluminum alloys. Below that, use Johnson's parabola or the tangent-modulus (Engesser) method, which the sheet mentions for 'yield buckling'.
  • Buckling depends on E and I, not strength.

cards.q: Pressure vessels, plates, and spinning parts
cards.a:
Thin sphere (R ≫ t): σ_hoop = σ₁ = σ₂ = PR/(2t), radial ≈ −P (small). Radial growth ΔR = PR²(1 − ν)/(2Et). Thermal growth ΔR = RαΔT. Stored energy U = πP²R⁴(1 − ν)/(Et).

Pipe with end caps: σ_axial ≈ PR/(2t); σ_hoop ≈ PR/t (thin wall, R_mean/t > 10). Thick wall, hoop at the bore: σ_hoop = P(Ro² + Ri²)/(Ro² − Ri²). Length change ΔL = (PRL/Et)(½ − ν), which is small because Poisson contraction from the hoop stress cancels most of the axial stretch. Radial growth ΔR = (PR²/Et)(1 − ν/2).

Flat circular plate, clamped edge, pressure P: center deflection δ = (3/16)·PR⁴(1 − ν²)/(Et³); max stress at the edge σ = (3/4)·P(R/t)².

Thermal stress, thin cylinder wall with temperature difference ΔT through the wall: σ = αEΔT/(2(1 − ν)).

Spinning disk or shaft, radial growth at the outer radius: Δr_o = ρω²r_o/(4E)·[(1 − ν)r_o² + (3 + ν)r_i²].

Interview notes

  • Hoop is twice axial, so cylinders split lengthwise (hot dog question).
  • Plate stress goes with (R/t)²: halving the thickness quadruples stress and makes it 8× more flexible.
  • Check the spinning-disk growth formula on the original sheet: the r_o² and r_i² terms must be as written here (it comes from the annular-disk solution).

cards.q: Fatigue, fracture, and margin of safety
cards.a:
• Low-cycle fatigue (part yields each cycle) below about 10⁴ cycles; high-cycle (elastic) above.
  • Manson universal slopes (strain-life estimate): Δε ≈ 3.5(σ_u/E)·N^−0.12 + [ln(1/(1 − RA))]^0.6·N^−0.6, where RA is the reduction in area. Gives total strain range for life N.
  • Hole in an infinite plate: elliptical hole with half-axes a (perpendicular to load) and b: K_t = 1 + 2a/b (circle: 3).
  • Stress intensity: large plate center crack K_I = σ√(πa); edge crack 1.12σ√(πa); center crack in a finite plate of width W: K_I = σ√(πa·sec(πa/W)).
  • Crack growth (Paris law): da/dN = C·ΔK^m. No growth below ΔK_threshold; fast fracture when K reaches K_IC.
  • Margin of safety: MS = Allowable/(Applied × FS) − 1, with FS the product of all applicable factors (ultimate × casting × thermal...). MS ≥ 0 passes.

Interview notes

  • Say 'margin of safety 0.23', not 'margin 1.23'. MS = 0 means exactly at the allowable with the factor applied.
  • Integrating the Paris law from the initial crack size to the critical crack size gives the number of cycles: that's how inspection intervals are set.

cards.q: Single-degree-of-freedom systems: frequency, damping, response
cards.a:
• Equation of motion: F(t) = mẍ + bẋ + kx, or F/m = ẍ + 2ζω_n ẋ + ω_n² x.
  • Natural frequency: ω_n = √(k/m) rad/s, f_n = (1/2π)√(k/m) Hz. It's the stiffness-to-mass ratio.
  • Damped frequency: ω_d = ω_n√(1 − ζ²), so ω_d ≈ ω_n for lightly damped structures.
  • Resonant amplification Q = A_max/A_static = 1/(2ζ). Doubling damping halves the peak.
  • Typical damping: ζ ≈ 1% bare metal structures, 2–3% with silicone/elastomer damping, 5–10% with fluid damping.
  • Step response: envelope Ae^(−ζω_n t); 1% settling time t_s ≈ 4.6/(ζω_n); overshoot = e^(−πζ/√(1 − ζ²)).
  • Estimate ζ from test data by fitting Ae^(−ζω_n t) to the decay (log decrement).

Interview notes

  • With 1% damping, Q = 50: a structure driven at resonance responds 50× its static deflection. That's why you keep natural frequencies away from forcing frequencies.
  • If using lbm in US units, divide mass by 386 in/s² to get consistent units (lbf·s²/in).

cards.q: Natural frequency formulas (fundamental mode)
cards.a:
Systemf₁ (Hz)
Mass m on a massless spring k(1/2π)√(k/m)
Mass m on a spring with mass m_s(1/2π)√(k/(m + m_s/3))
Tip mass m on a cantilever (beam mass m_b)(√3/2π)√(EI/((m + 0.24m_b)L³))
Center mass on a pinned-pinned beam(4√3/2π)√(EI/((m + 0.49m_b)L³))

A beam in tension stiffens: multiply f by √(1 + F_tension/F_buckling). Compression does the opposite and drives f to zero at the buckling load. (Source on the sheet: Blevins, Formulas for Natural Frequency and Mode Shape.)

Interview notes

  • The pattern: f ∝ √(stiffness/mass), and each beam case is just its static stiffness (3EI/L³, 48EI/L³, 192EI/L³) with an effective share of the beam's own mass added.
  • Where the constants come from: (√3/2π)√(EI/(mL³)) is just (1/2π)√((3EI/L³)/m), and 4√3 = √48, 8√3 = √192.

subs.title: Fluids, Gas Dynamics, and Heat Transfer

cards.q: Fluid mechanics
cards.a:
• Continuity: ρAU = constant = ṁ
  • Bernoulli (incompressible, inviscid, steady, along a streamline): P/ρ + U²/2 + gz = constant
  • Energy (adiabatic, steady, no work): c_p(T₂ − T₁) + (U₂² − U₁²)/2 + g(z₂ − z₁) = 0
  • Momentum on a control volume: ΣF = Σ(ṁV)_out − Σ(ṁV)_in, including pressure × area on the boundaries
  • Reynolds Re = ρUD/μ = UD/ν = 4ṁ/(πDμ) for a pipe. Nusselt Nu = hD/k. Prandtl Pr = ν/α.
  • Orifice or restriction: ṁ = C_d·A·√(2ρΔP_total)
  • Pipe pressure loss: ΔP = f·(L/D)·(ρU²/2); laminar f = 64/Re (turbulent: Moody chart)
  • Hydraulic diameter: D_h = 4A/P (area over wetted perimeter)
  • Cavitation index: K = 2ΔP/(ρU²); cavitation tends to start around K ≈ 0.2–1.5 depending on geometry

Interview notes

  • For interviews, Bernoulli and the control-volume momentum equation do most of the work (pitot tube, pipe bend forces, nozzle thrust).

cards.q: Gas dynamics and compressible flow
cards.a:
• Ideal gas: P = ρRT, R = R_u/MW, R_u = 8.314 J/(mol·K). Good for a first cut; use a compressibility factor when very cold (below about −100°F) or high pressure (above about 1,000 psia).
  • Adiabatic = no heat flow. Isentropic = adiabatic and reversible (no viscous losses).
  • Isentropic relations: P₂/P₁ = (ρ₂/ρ₁)^γ = (T₂/T₁)^(γ/(γ−1))
  • Total pressure (incompressible form): P_t = P + ρU²/2
  • Mach number M = U/√(γRT) (speed of sound √(γRT))
  • Flow is choked when P_t/P_∞ ≥ ((γ + 1)/2)^(γ/(γ−1)): about 1.9 for air, 1.7 for combustion gas
  • γ = 5/3 monatomic (He, Ne, Xe), 7/5 diatomic (N₂, O₂, air), about 1.1–1.25 for combustion gases

Interview notes

  • Choked means the throat has reached Mach 1; lowering the downstream pressure further can't increase the mass flow. The inverse, p*/p₀ ≈ 0.53 for air, is the other way it's quoted.

cards.q: Heat transfer
cards.a:
• Energy into a flow: Q = ṁ·c_p·ΔT
  • Conduction: Q = −kA·ΔT/Δx
  • Convection: Q = hA(T_s − T_∞)
  • Radiation: Q = F·ε·σ·A(T_s⁴ − T_∞⁴), σ = 5.67×10⁻⁸ W/(m²K⁴), F = view factor, temperatures in kelvin
  • Re = ρVL/μ, Nu = hL/k_fluid, Biot Bi = hL/k_solid (Bi < 0.1: the solid is nearly uniform in temperature, so lumped analysis works)

Interview notes

  • In space there's no convection, so radiation (and conduction to a radiator) is how heat leaves.
  • Nusselt and Biot look the same but use different k: fluid for Nu, solid for Bi.

cards.q: Rocket mechanics
cards.a:
• Thrust: T = ṁV_e + (P_e − P_∞)A_e = C_F·P_c·A_t = I_sp·ṁ·g₀
  • Thrust coefficient (momentum part): C_F = √{(2γ²/(γ − 1))·(2/(γ + 1))^((γ+1)/(γ−1))·[1 − (P_e/P_c)^((γ−1)/γ)]}, plus (P_e − P_∞)/P_c × A_e/A_t for the pressure term (in vacuum, P_∞ = 0)
  • Rocket equation: ΔV = V_e·ln(m_initial/m_final)
  • Area-Mach relation (pressure along the nozzle from the area): A_t/A = ((γ + 1)/2)^((γ+1)/(2(γ−1)))·M / (1 + ((γ − 1)/2)M²)^((γ+1)/(2(γ−1)))
  • Chamber region Mach about 0.2, throat M = 1, exit typically M ≈ 3–5
  • Free-body of the chamber: tension in the chamber/nozzle structure = P_c·A_c − T

Interview notes

  • I_sp (seconds) is thrust per unit weight flow; V_e = I_sp·g₀.
  • The rocket equation's log is why staging helps: dropping dead mass raises the mass ratio of what's left.
  • Thrust is maximized when the nozzle is ideally expanded (P_e = P_∞).

cards.q: Orbital mechanics
cards.a:
• Circular orbit speed: V = r₀√(g₀/(r₀ + h)) ≈ √(g₀r₀) in low orbit (about 7.9 km/s)
  • Escape speed from the surface: √(2g₀r₀) ≈ 11.2 km/s
  • Period: τ = 2π(r₀ + h)^(3/2)/(r₀√g₀) ≈ 2π√(r₀/g₀) ≈ 84 min at the surface; about 90 min for the ISS
  • Same form as a pendulum: τ = 2π√(L/g)
  • g₀ = 9.81 m/s² (Earth), 3.71 m/s² (Mars). Earth radius r₀ = 6.37×10⁶ m
  • Altitudes: ISS about 4×10⁵ m; geostationary about 3.6×10⁷ m; Mars at closest about 5.5×10¹⁰ m away

Interview notes

  • Escape speed is √2 times orbital speed at the same radius.

cards.q: Math shortcuts
cards.a:
• Small angles (θ < ~15°): sin θ ≈ θ, cos θ ≈ 1 − θ²/2, tan θ ≈ θ (radians; 1 rad ≈ 57.3°)
  • Binomial: (1 + ε)ⁿ ≈ 1 + nε for small ε, so 1/(1 + ε) ≈ 1 − ε and 1/(1 − ε) ≈ 1 + ε
  • Law of cosines: c² = a² + b² − 2ab·cos C
  • Tube area: π(Ro² − Ri²) ≈ 2πRt (thin wall). Tube surface: πDL. Sphere surface: 4πR². Ellipse: πab. Spherical shell volume: (4/3)π(Ro³ − Ri³)

Interview notes

  • The binomial shortcut is how you get things like 'a 1% increase in diameter gives about a 4% increase in I' (I ∝ D⁴).

cards.a:

cards.q: Interview format
cards.a: Based on past candidate reports: the interviews are mostly technical, built around your projects and the job posting. Expect intuition questions like the tape measure, steel vs aluminum density, and the other physical-reasoning questions in this doc. They care more about your thought process than getting every answer right, so think out loud and state assumptions.

cards.q: What do you know about our team?
cards.a: Booster Structures owns the primary load-bearing structure of the first stage: the tanks, thrust structure, interstage, and the interfaces to propulsion and landing systems. These parts have to survive extreme loads during ascent, stage separation, reentry, and landing while staying as light as possible. The work is tightly tied to manufacturing and testing because of the hardware's size and the push for fast iteration, so it involves a lot of welded structures, large-scale fabrication, structural analysis, and full-scale testing. Because the booster is reused, durability over many flights and ease of inspection are also major design drivers.

cards.q: Why SpaceX?
cards.a: A big reason I went into engineering was to work on problems that matter, and I try to pick projects that prepare me to make that kind of impact. SpaceX stands out because the mission is ambitious but grounded in real hardware and real results. I respect what other aerospace companies do, but what draws me to SpaceX specifically is the pace: fast design-build-test cycles where failures are treated as data and the next iteration is already being built. Many organizations work on long timelines with few full-system tests. At SpaceX, engineers learn faster and see the direct impact of their work, and that's where I'd grow and contribute the most.

cards.q: Why aerospace?
cards.a: It started with Star Wars. I grew up in the prequel era, and as a kid I fully believed everything in the movies and The Clone Wars was happening somewhere out there. As I got older I realized those stories weren't real, but they left me curious about what actually is out there and how far people can go. That curiosity shifted from imagination to engineering: instead of wondering whether those worlds exist, I got interested in the real technology that could let us explore. What keeps me interested now is the challenge of turning science fiction into real hardware.

cards.q: What is SpaceX's mission?
cards.a: To make humanity multiplanetary. In practice, that means developing fully reusable launch systems and the infrastructure to sustain human life beyond Earth, starting with Mars.

cards.q: What do you bring?
cards.a:
Hands-on structural design experience from concept through fabrication and testing. Across Baja SAE, combat robotics, and my internship at Advanced Spade, I've designed load-bearing parts, validated them with FEA, machined them myself, and tested them in real conditions, so I know how designs behave outside of CAD and how to iterate when something doesn't work the first time.

I'm comfortable designing under tight constraints: a 12 lb weapon allocation on a 30 lb robot, a gimbal redesign that had to shrink 53%, and a Baja suspension system that had to get 10% lighter on a fixed budget. I also lead people. I run a 13-person suspension subteam and defend our design in formal reviews. And I'm used to cross-functional work where mechanical hardware has to integrate with electrical and software. Launch vehicle structures combine extreme loads, weight sensitivity, and manufacturability, which are exactly the challenges I've enjoyed most.

cards.q: Questions to ask SpaceX
cards.a:
• How are new engineers brought into the team's workflow, and what does success look like in the first six months?
  • What are the biggest technical challenges the team is facing right now?
  • What types of structures would I most likely work on?
  • How closely does the design team work with technicians on the floor, and what's that dynamic like?
  • What knowledge do you wish new hires already had?

subs.title: SpaceX: Questions I Was Actually Asked

cards.q: A cantilever with a uniform cross-section has a downward point load at its free end. You keep pushing until it breaks. Where does it break?
cards.a:
At the fixed end (the wall). The bending moment grows linearly from zero at the tip to M = PL at the root, and since the cross-section is uniform, the bending stress σ = Mc/I is highest where the moment is highest. Shear is constant along the length (V = P), and for a slender beam the shear stress is small compared with the bending stress, so bending governs.

In a real part it's even more likely at the root, because that's where the clamp, weld, or fillet adds a stress concentration.

Follow-ups

  • If it's short and deep, shear can matter: check τ = 1.5V/A at the neutral axis.
  • The deflection at the tip is PL³/3EI, but deflection doesn't tell you where it breaks.

cards.q: Would it break at the top or the bottom of the beam?
cards.a:
With a downward tip load, the beam bends concave-down: the top fibers stretch (tension) and the bottom fibers squash (compression), with the same magnitude for a symmetric section. Most materials fail first on the tension side, so I'd expect the crack to start at the top surface at the wall.

Why tension: brittle materials (cast iron, ceramics, glass, concrete) are much weaker in tension, so they crack at the top. Ductile metals yield top and bottom at about the same time, but the actual fracture still starts on the tension side, where cracks open up and grow; the compression side just yields and bulges.

Follow-ups

  • Exceptions: fiber composites and wood can fail first on the compression side (fiber microbuckling or crushing), and thin-walled sections can buckle locally on the compression side before anything yields. That's the setup for the next question.
  • Say the reasoning out loud: 'top is tension, bottom is compression, and tension is what opens cracks.'

cards.q: What material property do you need to know to predict when it breaks?
cards.a:
The strength. For 'breaks' meaning fracture, the ultimate tensile strength (for a brittle material, the modulus of rupture or flexural strength). If 'failure' means permanent bending, the yield strength. Set σ = Mc/I = PLc/I equal to the strength and solve: P = σ_strength·I/(L·c).

Young's modulus is the trap answer. E tells you how much it deflects, not when it breaks.

Follow-ups

  • Ductile beams don't stop at first yield. The section keeps carrying load until it's fully plastic (a plastic hinge), at Mp = σy·Z. For a rectangle Z = 1.5·S, so it carries about 50% more moment than first yield. That's why ductility (elongation) also matters.
  • If the beam has cracks or flaws, you also need fracture toughness K_IC.
  • The other inputs are geometry: L, I, and c.

cards.q: Now make it a thin-walled hollow tube. Does the failure mode change?
cards.a:
Yes, it can. A thin-walled tube is very efficient in bending because the material sits far from the neutral axis, but its walls are thin. The compression side at the root (the bottom) can buckle locally, wrinkling or kinking inward, before the material ever reaches yield. So instead of yielding or cracking on the top, it fails by local buckling on the bottom.

Whether it happens depends on the diameter-to-thickness ratio: the classical local buckling stress for a thin cylinder is about 0.6·E·t/R (and real tubes buckle well below that because of imperfections, typically 30–60% of it). If that's below yield, buckling wins. A thicker wall goes back to the solid-beam behavior.

Follow-ups

  • Thin tubes in bending also ovalize (the Brazier effect): the cross-section flattens, I drops, and it can collapse suddenly.
  • Picture crushing a soda can or bending a drinking straw: it kinks on the inside of the bend.
  • Fixes: thicker wall, stiffening rings or stringers, or filling the tube (foam core).

cards.q: Back to a solid beam that only ever sees a downward load. What shape gives the best mass efficiency?
cards.a:
An I-beam with the web vertical. Bending stiffness and strength come from I, and an I-beam puts most of its material in the flanges, far from the neutral axis, with a thin web holding them apart and carrying the shear. For the same mass it has several times the I of a solid rectangle.

Then taper it along the length. The moment is zero at the tip and PL at the wall, so a uniform beam is overbuilt everywhere except the root. A tapered beam that's deep at the wall and shallow at the tip keeps the stress near the allowable all along the length (a 'fully stressed' beam) and drops a lot of mass. For constant width, depth ∝ √x; for constant depth, width ∝ x.

Follow-ups

  • Limits on the I-beam: thin flanges can buckle locally, the compression flange can buckle sideways (lateral-torsional buckling), and the web has to carry shear without buckling.
  • Even lighter: a truss, which turns bending into axial forces in members.
  • Because it only loads one way, a symmetric I-beam is fine; if it only ever sees tension on top, you could use a T or bias material toward the side that needs it.

cards.q: What if the load were torsion instead? What shape is most mass-efficient?
cards.a:
A thin-walled closed circular tube. Torsional shear stress grows linearly from zero at the center to a maximum at the surface (τ = Tr/J), so material near the center does almost nothing. A tube puts all the material at the outside radius, where it works hardest, and the closed shape lets shear flow all the way around. The I-beam is the worst choice here: open thin sections are terrible in torsion.

Follow-ups

  • Open vs closed: slit the same tube lengthwise and it gets about 3(r/t)² times less stiff, 300× at r/t = 10.
  • Limit: very thin walls buckle in torsion, in diagonal wrinkles, so there's a practical minimum thickness.
  • Real examples: drive shafts, torque tubes, and the reason car chassis use closed box sections.

cards.q: Two concentric tubes of equal length and equal cross-sectional area, not touching, welded at both ends to rigid plates. Inner is aluminum; outer is steel with 3× the diameter. Pull the plates apart. Which tube carries more force?
cards.a:
The steel (outer) tube. The rigid plates force both tubes to stretch the same amount, so they have the same strain. Force = E·A·ε, and the areas are equal, so each tube's share is proportional to its modulus. Steel's E (about 200 GPa) is about 3 times aluminum's (about 70 GPa), so steel carries about 3/4 of the load and aluminum about 1/4.

The diameter doesn't matter for axial load: only area, modulus, and length do. That's a distractor (it matters later for buckling). Same idea as the three-legged table: parallel load paths share load by stiffness.

Follow-ups

  • Equivalent stiffness of the pair is k = (E_s + E_a)·A/L, like two springs in parallel.
  • Stresses: the steel stress is about 3× the aluminum stress at every load.

cards.q: Keep pulling until one fails. Which fails first?
cards.a:
Compare strains, not stresses, because the plates force the strain to be the same in both. Each tube yields when the shared strain reaches its own yield strain, σy/E. Mild steel: 250 MPa / 200 GPa ≈ 0.125%. 6061-T6 aluminum: 276 MPa / 69 GPa ≈ 0.4%. So the steel yields first, even though it's stronger, because it's so much stiffer that it reaches its yield strain sooner.

After the steel yields it stops picking up load, and the extra load shifts to the aluminum until it yields too. For final fracture, it's whichever runs out of ductility first. Mild steel stretches 20%+ before breaking, 6061-T6 about 10–12%, so the aluminum probably fractures first.

So my answer: steel yields first, aluminum likely breaks first, and I'd want to know the exact alloys, because a high-strength steel (yield strain 0.5% or more) flips the first part.

Follow-ups

  • The welds: welding 6061 turns the heat-affected zone near the weld much softer than T6 (often around half the strength). In practice the aluminum's weld zone could be the first thing to go.
  • Showing the strain logic is what they're looking for. 'Steel is stronger so aluminum fails' is the trap.

cards.q: Push the plates together instead (compression). Does anything change?
cards.a:
In the elastic range, nothing: same strain, same 3:1 split, with steel carrying about 74%. Yield in compression is about the same as in tension for these metals, so the steel still yields first. What changes is that compression brings in buckling, which tension can't.

Follow-ups

  • Fracture isn't really a compression failure mode for ductile metals; they squash or buckle instead.

cards.q: If buckling is a concern, how does that change your answer?
cards.a:
Now geometry matters, including the 3× diameter. Two kinds of buckling compete.

Global (Euler) column buckling: the aluminum tube goes first. Both tubes see the same strain, and a column buckles when its strain reaches π²r_g²/L_e², where r_g is its radius of gyration. E cancels out, so only the size matters. With equal areas, the steel tube's 3× diameter gives it 9× the I/A, so it can take 9× the strain before buckling. The skinny aluminum tube buckles first, and when it does, its load sheds to the steel.

Local (shell) wall buckling: the steel tube goes first. For thin walls, equal area at 3× the diameter means the steel wall is 1/3 as thick, so its t/R is 1/9 of the aluminum's. Local buckling strain is about 0.6·t/R (again E cancels), so the thin-walled steel tube wrinkles at about 1/9 the strain.

So: long, slender tubes, the inner aluminum buckles globally first. Short tubes with thin walls, the outer steel wrinkles locally first. I'd check both against yield and see which one comes first for the actual length and wall thickness.

Follow-ups

  • Being welded to rigid plates at both ends makes both tubes roughly fixed-fixed (K = 0.5), the best case for Euler buckling.
  • If the inner tube buckles sideways it would hit the outer tube, which then braces it. Worth mentioning as a real-world wrinkle.

cards.q: Now no load: heat the whole assembly by 250°F. What happens?
cards.a:
The aluminum wants to grow about twice as much as the steel (α ≈ 23×10⁻⁶/°C vs 12×10⁻⁶/°C), but the rigid plates make both end up the same length. So the aluminum is held back (compression) and the steel is pulled along (tension). With no external load, the forces have to cancel, and with equal areas the stresses are equal and opposite.

Compatibility: α_a·ΔT + σ_a/E_a = α_s·ΔT + σ_s/E_s, with σ_a = −σ_s. So σ_s = (α_a − α_s)·ΔT / (1/E_s + 1/E_a). For ΔT = 250°F (139°C): (11×10⁻⁶)(139) = 1.53×10⁻³ of mismatch strain, divided by (1/200 + 1/70) GPa⁻¹, gives about 79 MPa (11.5 ksi): steel in tension, aluminum in compression. Heating from 70°F to 250°F (a 180°F rise) gives about 57 MPa (8 ksi).

The assembly grows by an amount in between the two free expansions: effective α = (E_a·α_a + E_s·α_s)/(E_a + E_s) ≈ 15×10⁻⁶/°C, closer to steel's because steel is stiffer.

Follow-ups

  • That stress isn't enough to yield either tube, but it adds to mechanical loads: under tension, the aluminum's thermal pre-compression delays its yield and the steel yields even sooner.
  • Aluminum in compression means the inner tube's buckling margin drops.
  • Cooling reverses everything: aluminum in tension, steel in compression.
  • The welds and plates carry the shear that transfers this force; that's where thermal fatigue cracks would show up under repeated heating cycles.
  • Aluminum alloys lose strength at elevated temperature; 250°F is mild for 6061-T6, but long exposure above about 300°F starts to soften it.
